examples.analytical: The essay describes a somnolent society that accepts its own stagnation without protest.

nuance.analogy: A somnolent atmosphere is like a lake on a windless day: still, quiet, and easy to drift into.
nuance.etymology: From Latin somnolentus, sleepy.
common_mistakes: Using somnolent for a person who is simply tired in a casual conversation; sleepy is more natural.
Pronouncing the middle as 'SAHM-no-lent', dropping the schwa.

senses.definition: In a somnolent way; sleepily.

core.definition: In a drowsy, sleepy manner; while feeling sleepy or half-asleep.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, and the -ent- is a weak, unstressed syllable. The final -ly is pronounced lee, not 'lie'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and descriptive. It evokes a calm, sleepy mood and is often used in fiction.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use somnolently mainly in literary and descriptive writing, not in everyday talk. In conversation they would say sleepily or drowsily. The adverb sounds deliberate and slightly formal, so use it when you want a sense of lazy, half-asleep calm.

distinctions.note: Sleepily is the common, everyday adverb; somnolently is more formal and literary and suggests a lingering drowsy state.
Drowsily is also common in ordinary speech; somnolently is more elevated and is mostly used in writing.

examples.professional: By four o'clock the call had gone quiet, and people were nodding somnolently through the slides.
examples.analytical: A writer might describe the valley lying somnolently under the noon sun, as if time itself had slowed.

nuance.analogy: Like a lazy river moving so slowly that it seems to be asleep.
nuance.etymology: From somnolent, from Latin somnolentus 'sleepy', with the adverbial suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Confusing somnolently with somnambulantly, which refers to sleepwalking.
Using somnolently in casual conversation, where sleepily sounds more natural.

core.definition: A title Jesus uses for himself in the Gospels, drawn from Daniel 7, pointing to his true humanity and to his divine authority, suffering and coming glory.

pronunciation.tip: Stress SUN and MAN, and reduce 'of' to a weak 'uv'. The title is said as three quick words, with the 'of' almost disappearing.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this title mainly in church, Bible study and theology, not in everyday talk. In a sermon or a Bible class, it is normally capitalized and refers to Jesus. Outside religious settings, the phrase may sound odd or simply mean 'a human being' in older English.

distinctions.note: Son of God stresses Jesus' divinity and unique relationship with the Father, while Son of Man stresses his humanity and his role as the representative of humankind.
In Ezekiel, God addresses the prophet as 'son of man' simply to mean 'mortal'; the capitalized title in the Gospels carries a messianic meaning.

collocations: the Son of Man coming in glory
Jesus called himself the Son of Man

examples.everyday: My Bible study group spent the whole evening talking about what Jesus meant when he called himself the Son of Man.
examples.professional: In my lecture on the Gospels, I always explain the Son of Man sayings before we discuss the passion narratives.
examples.analytical: The Son of Man in Daniel 7 is a heavenly figure who receives dominion, and the Gospels reshape that image to join authority with suffering.

nuance.analogy: Like a name that means both 'a regular person' and 'the one who speaks for all people', the title holds humanity and divine mission together.
nuance.etymology: From Hebrew ben adam, 'son of man', meaning a human being; in Greek, huios tou anthropou.
common_mistakes: Dropping the capital letters, which changes a christological title into a generic phrase.
Pronouncing 'of' fully as 'off' instead of the weak 'uv'.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew is ben adam (בֶּן־אָדָם), meaning 'son of man' or 'human being'; the Aramaic bar enash lies behind some Gospel sayings, and the Greek is huios tou anthropou. Daniel 7:13 (RSV) describes 'one like a son of man' coming with the clouds of heaven to receive an everlasting dominion. Mark 2:10 records Jesus saying that the Son of man has authority on earth to forgive sins. Mark 8:31 says the Son of man must suffer, be rejected and be killed, and rise again.

senses.definition: Something or someone who makes a sound.
senses.example: a telephone with an electronic sounder

senses.definition: An instrument used in telegraphy in place of a register, the communications being read by sound.
senses.example: The old telegraph operator listened to the sounder clicking out messages all afternoon.

senses.definition: Synonym of sting (“brief musical sequence in television etc.”).
senses.example: The producers wrote a short sounder to introduce each segment of the news program.

senses.definition: A fishfinder.
senses.example: We marked the school of bass on the boat's sounder before casting our lines.

senses.definition: A group of wild boar.
senses.example: A sounder of wild boar crossed the creek at dawn, leaving tracks in the mud.

senses.definition: A young boar.
senses.example: The farm dog chased the young sounder back toward the pasture gate.

senses.definition: A device for making soundings at sea.
A person who takes soundings.
senses.example: The harbor sounder shouted depth readings to the captain as the ship entered the channel.

senses.definition: (dated) A stethoscope.
senses.example: The old doctor pressed his sounder to my chest and listened for a long while.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: Something, such as a device or alarm, that makes a sound to signal or alert people.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable. The final -er is a weak, r-colored syllable, so say 'SOWN-dur,' not 'SOWN-dah.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a functional object or person without praise or criticism.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'sounder' in everyday speech. For a common device, they say 'alarm,' 'buzzer,' 'beeper' or 'horn.' The word appears mostly in technical contexts such as building systems, telegraph history and engineering specifications.

distinctions.note: A horn is a specific loud device, while sounder is a general term for anything that makes a sound as a signal.
Sound is the sensation or vibration that reaches the ear, while sounder is the thing that produces it.

examples.everyday: The sounder on the smoke detector beeps whenever the battery is low.
examples.professional: We replaced the faulty sounder on the server rack so technicians hear failures immediately.
examples.analytical: In the early telegraph system, the operator relied on the sounder rather than a paper register, reading messages by ear.

nuance.analogy: A sounder is like a doorbell that exists only to announce that something needs attention.
nuance.etymology: From sound (from Latin sonus through Old French son) plus the agent suffix -er.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'sounder' with 'sound' when referring to a device, since the device is the sounder.
Pronouncing the final -er as a full 'ah' sound, as in 'SOWN-dah.'

sounder.etymology: From Middle English **soundere*, from Old English *ġesundra*, from Proto-Germanic **sundizô*, equivalent to *sound* + *er*.

senses.definition: The critical evaluation of a source of information in terms of intent, date, bias, authenticity and reliability by means of the methodologies of the humanities.

core.definition: The scholarly method of evaluating a source's date, author, purpose, bias, and reliability before using its information.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on KRIT in criticism. Sources is one syllable in careful speech, and the r in sawrs is clearly pronounced in American English.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a scholarly term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use source criticism mainly in academic writing, history, journalism, and biblical studies. In everyday speech they might say checking your sources. The term does not mean finding fault; critical here means careful evaluation.

distinctions.note: Fact-checking tests specific claims against evidence; source criticism evaluates the origin and reliability of the source itself.
Textual criticism studies the wording of manuscripts to recover the original text; source criticism examines where a text's information came from.

examples.everyday: My history teacher said I need to do some source criticism before I cite that website.
examples.professional: Before we rely on the vendor's report, the analyst should apply source criticism to check its date and funding.
examples.analytical: Source criticism of the Pentateuch identifies several strands whose origins and purposes must be weighed against one another.

nuance.analogy: Like checking a restaurant review: you ask who wrote it, when, and whether they had a reason to be biased before trusting it.
nuance.etymology: Source comes from Old French sourse, from Latin surgere, to rise; criticism comes from Greek kritikos, able to judge.
common_mistakes: Assuming criticism means attacking a source; here it means careful evaluation.
Stressing the wrong syllable in criticism; the stress falls on KRIT, not on -ism.
nuance.biblical_note: Source criticism in biblical studies asks which written documents or traditions stand behind a biblical book. The Bible itself points to sources: Numbers 21:14 refers to the Book of the Wars of the Lord, and 1 Kings 14:19 cites the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel. Luke 1:1-4 says the evangelist investigated earlier accounts before writing, which scholars use to study how the Gospels were composed.

senses.definition: A type of bread dough leavened with yeast and lactobacilli that produce acids giving a sour taste.
senses.example: I bake a sourdough loaf every Sunday, feeding my starter the night before.

senses.definition: An old-timer, especially in Alaska.
senses.example: The sourdoughs at the bar swapped stories about the winters they survived up north.

senses.definition: A permanent resident of the territory. Someone who has lived in the Yukon during all four seasons.
senses.example: Only a true sourdough would think a minus-forty morning worth a walk to town.

senses.definition: A 49er, a California Gold Rush miner.
senses.example: Her great-grandfather arrived in California as a sourdough, digging for gold along the American River.

core.definition: Bread made from a dough that is leavened with a fermented starter of wild yeast and bacteria, giving it a tangy flavor.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SOUR, and the second syllable is a reduced 'er'. Say the first syllable as 'sow' in 'cow', not 'sore'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests artisanal, flavorful and wholesome bread.
nuance.usage_note: Americans buy sourdough at grocery stores, bakeries and farmers markets, and they often ask for 'a loaf of sourdough' or 'sourdough toast.' In Alaska and the Yukon, sourdough also means an old-timer, but that sense is regional. In a restaurant, sourdough usually means the bread is served as a side.

distinctions.note: White bread is usually made with commercial yeast and has a mild flavor. Sourdough has a tangy, acidic taste from its fermented starter.
Rye bread is made mainly with rye flour, and it may or may not be sourdough. Sourdough describes the leavening method.
A baguette is a shape of bread, usually leavened with yeast. Sourdough describes a fermentation method, so a sourdough baguette is possible.

examples.everyday: Can you grab a loaf of sourdough on your way home?
examples.professional: The café's sourdough supplier is running late, so we'll switch to baguettes for the lunch menu.
examples.analytical: Sourdough reveals how bread can be a living culture, with wild microbes shaping flavor across generations of starter.

nuance.analogy: Like a family recipe passed down through generations, where a living starter carries the flavor forward.
nuance.etymology: From sour, from Old English sūr, plus dough, from Old English dāh.
common_mistakes: Writing sour dough as two words in informal notes; in American usage, it is usually one word.
Pronouncing the first syllable like 'sore'; it sounds like 'sow'.

sourdough.etymology: From Middle English *sour dogh*, equivalent to *sour* + *dough*.

senses.definition: Of, relating to, or affected by spasm.
Of or relating to spastic paralysis.
Incompetent or physically uncoordinated.
senses.example: Stop being so spastic with that ball, you keep dropping everything!

senses.definition: Hyperactive or behaving erratically.
senses.example: The toddler got spastic after eating too much candy at the party.

core.definition: Affected by spasms or by stiff, involuntary muscle tightening, as in spastic paralysis.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the -tic ending is short and unstressed. Keep the st cluster sharp, without an extra vowel after the s.

nuance.connotation: Negative when used about people, because it is a slur in everyday speech. In medicine it is neutral and clinical.
nuance.usage_note: Doctors use spastic in medical terms such as spastic paralysis or spastic muscles, and it appears in some older medical writing. Americans avoid calling a person spastic, because it is offensive; the term spaz is also an insult. In normal conversation, describe the condition specifically, such as 'muscle stiffness' or 'a movement disorder.'

distinctions.note: Spasmodic describes sudden, irregular bursts of movement, while spastic describes persistent stiffness or contraction of muscles.
In everyday speech, calling a person spastic is an insult meaning clumsy or uncoordinated, and it should be avoided.

examples.everyday: My neighbor's son has a condition that makes his leg muscles stiff, so I try to describe it in plain words.
examples.professional: The physical therapist said the spastic muscles in his arm need daily stretching and gentle exercise.
examples.analytical: The phrase spastic paralysis names a specific clinical pattern, though the term has taken on demeaning uses in ordinary speech.

nuance.analogy: Like a stiff hinge that will not swing smoothly, the muscle stays tight and resists movement.
nuance.etymology: From Greek spastikos, 'drawing,' related to spasm.
common_mistakes: Using spastic as a casual insult for clumsiness, which is offensive.
Confusing spastic with spasmodic, which describes irregular bursts rather than stiffness.

senses.definition: Spherical.
Of or relating to the heavenly orbs, or to the sphere or spheres in which, according to ancient astronomy and astrology, they were set.
senses.example: Medieval astronomers believed the spheric realms of the planets rotated around a fixed Earth.

core.definition: Having the shape of a sphere; spherical. It is rare and mostly literary in modern American English.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The sf starts together, and the vowel is the 'air' sound of 'fair'. Don't say an extra syllable as in 'sphe-ri-ka'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It sounds poetic or old-fashioned compared with spherical.
nuance.usage_note: Americans almost always say spherical in everyday, scientific, and technical contexts. Spheric sounds poetic or antiquated, so using it in conversation may sound affected. You will mostly see it in older texts or in poetry.

distinctions.note: Spherical is the standard word in modern English. Spheric is rarer and more literary.
A spheroid is a shape slightly flattened or stretched from a true sphere. Spheric describes an exact or ideal sphere.
Circular describes two dimensions, like a circle on a page. Spheric describes three dimensions.

examples.everyday: The old lamp had a spheric glass shade that looked like a big bubble.
examples.professional: The technician said the lens should be spheric, so the light spreads evenly across the sensor.
examples.analytical: Early cosmologists imagined the heavens as spheric shells that carried the planets around the earth.

nuance.analogy: Spheric is the poetic cousin of spherical, like a marble described in a poem instead of a catalog.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin sphaericus, from Greek sphairikos, from sphaira, meaning 'ball' or 'sphere'.
common_mistakes: Using spheric in everyday speech where Americans say round or spherical.
Stressing the second syllable (sfuh-RIK) instead of the first.

senses.definition: Like a spider.
Characterized by many spindly extensions.
senses.example: The spidery construction looked like it would fall apart in a stiff breeze.

senses.definition: Suggestive of cobwebs; spiderweb-like.
Infested with or containing many spiders.
Cramped or illegible; especially when spiky.
senses.example: Her handwriting was so spidery and cramped that the grader couldn't read half the answers.

core.definition: Long, thin and delicate, or spreading out in many thin lines, like a spider's legs or a spider's web.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle syllable is a quick, reduced r-colored sound, and the last syllable is a light 'ee' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative: it describes thin, uneven or fragile shapes, such as messy handwriting, and is rarely used as praise.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use spidery mainly in descriptive writing, for handwriting, drawings, branches or lines that look long and thin. It is less common in casual speech, and people usually say 'thin and spread out' or 'spindly' instead. For people, it is unusual and may sound odd unless used jokingly about long fingers or legs.

distinctions.note: Spindly describes something thin and weak, often a plant or a person's legs, while spidery focuses on the look of long lines spreading out.
Wiry describes something stiff, tough and thin like wire, often a person's build or hair, while spidery describes delicate, spreading lines.

examples.everyday: Grandma's handwriting is so spidery that I can barely read her birthday cards.
examples.professional: The chart's spidery lines made the trends hard to read, so I redrew it with thicker markers.
examples.analytical: The spidery network of citations shows how one idea branched into many disciplines over a century.

nuance.analogy: Spidery is like a sketch of a tree in winter: many thin branches reaching out in every direction.
nuance.etymology: From spider plus the suffix -y, meaning like a spider.
common_mistakes: Using spidery to describe a spider's body shape only; it usually describes thin, spreading lines or shapes.
Confusing spidery with spiky, which describes sharp points.

senses.definition: An act of deception; a hoax; a joking prank.
senses.example: Don't click anything on that website! That whole site is a spoof! Call IT right now.

senses.definition: A cyberattack involving deception via impersonated identities; a digital asset used in such an attack.
senses.example: Don't click anything on that website! That whole site is a spoof! Call IT right now.

senses.definition: A light parody.
Nonsense.
senses.example: Don't give me that spoof about the meeting being canceled; I saw you in the office.

senses.definition: A constructed number or solution that satisfies a set of conditions only when one of its rules are relaxed.
senses.example: The number that satisfied the equation was a spoof, valid only if we ignored the sign rule.

senses.definition: Fake, hoax.
senses.example: The company's award turned out to be a spoof certificate printed by a bored intern.

senses.definition: To gently satirize.
senses.example: The comedy show spoofs politicians every week, mocking their speeches with gentle exaggeration.

senses.definition: To deceive.
senses.example: He spoofed his roommate into believing the package contained a new laptop.

senses.definition: To falsify; especially, to falsify identities by impersonating for scamming purposes.
senses.example: The fraudsters convincingly spoofed a Microsoft webpage and then invited their victims to click various links found there.

core.definition: A playful parody or a harmless joke that imitates a movie, show or serious work in an exaggerated way.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is the long 'oo' of 'goof' and 'roof', not the short 'a' or 'o'. The 'f' at the end is clear.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive when it means a comedy parody; negative when it means a scam or a fake identity used to deceive.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use spoof for comedy films, TV sketches and online videos that imitate a famous work, as in 'a spoof of a superhero movie'. In tech and security, spoofing means faking an identity, such as a fake email address, so context matters. For a fraud, Americans may say hoax or scam instead.

distinctions.note: Parody is a more general or literary word for imitation, often with serious critical intent; spoof is lighter, more informal and more comic.
A hoax is a deliberate trick to fool people, often for real harm or publicity; a spoof is usually playful and meant to be recognized as a joke.

collocations: a spoof of a famous film

examples.everyday: Have you seen that spoof of the morning news? It is hilarious.
examples.professional: The security team flagged a phishing email that used a spoof of our CEO's address.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that the spoof works only when the audience recognizes the original it mocks.

nuance.analogy: A spoof is a funhouse mirror of a famous work: you recognize the original, but everything is stretched for laughs.
nuance.etymology: Late 19th-century English coinage; its origin is uncertain, though it is popularly linked to the comedian Arthur Roberts.
common_mistakes: Using spoof for a serious fraud; in that case, hoax or scam is the better word.
Pronouncing it with a short vowel, as in 'spof'.

senses.definition: The state or office of a stakeholder.

core.definition: The status or role of being a stakeholder, a person with a legitimate interest in an organization's decisions or results.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on STAKE, with a lighter secondary stress on -ship. The -er is a reduced r-colored vowel, so it sounds like 'der' and not 'dare'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise term in governance and business writing with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use stakeholdership in speech. They say 'stakeholder status' or 'being a stakeholder' instead. You will see it in corporate governance, policy papers and academic writing, so use it mainly in formal documents.

distinctions.note: Stakeholdership is the status or position of being a stakeholder, while stakeholding is the act or fact of holding a stake.
Stakeholder status is more natural in American speech and business writing, while stakeholdership sounds more academic.

examples.professional: Our governance policy defines stakeholdership for customers, employees and investors in each major decision.
examples.analytical: Democratic theory asks how stakeholdership should be distributed among citizens who bear the consequences of a policy.

nuance.analogy: Like being a co-owner of a shared garden: your interest is real even if you do not own the land.
nuance.etymology: Formed from stakeholder, a compound of stake and holder.
common_mistakes: Using stakeholdership in casual conversation, where 'being a stakeholder' sounds more natural.
Stressing the wrong syllable, which should be STAYK-hohl-der-ship.

senses.definition: A compartment for a single animal in a stable or cattle shed.
senses.example: The farmer moved the injured calf into an empty stall near the barn door.

senses.definition: A stable; a place for cattle.
senses.example: Before sunrise, the dairy workers led the cows back to the stall for milking.

senses.definition: A bench or table on which small articles of merchandise are exposed for sale.
senses.example: She arranged jars of honey and handmade soap on the stall at the farmers market.

senses.definition: A small open-fronted shop, for example in a market, food court, etc.
senses.example: The noodle stall in the food court has the longest line every lunchtime.

senses.definition: A small partitioned space or roomlet used for a shower or a toilet.
senses.example: The hotel's shower stall was so narrow that I could barely turn around.

senses.definition: A seat in a theater close to and (about) level with the stage; traditionally, a seat with arms, or otherwise partly enclosed, as distinguished from the benches, sofas, etc.
senses.example: We bought stall seats near the front, close enough to see the actors' expressions.

senses.definition: An Heathen altar, typically an indoor one, as contrasted with a more substantial outdoor harrow.
senses.example: Archaeologists uncovered a stone stall where ancient pagans had left offerings to their gods.

senses.definition: A seat in a church, especially one next to the chancel or choir, reserved for church officials and dignitaries.
senses.example: The bishop sat in the carved oak stall beside the choir during the service.

senses.definition: A church office that entitles the incumbent to the use of a church stall.
senses.example: He received a canonry and the stall that came with it at the cathedral.

senses.definition: A sheath to protect the finger.
senses.example: I covered my injured finger with a rubber stall before returning to the lab.

senses.definition: The space left by excavation between pillars.
senses.example: Miners left a stall between the pillars to support the roof of the chamber.

senses.definition: A parking stall; a space for a vehicle in a parking lot or parkade.
senses.example: Please park in your assigned stall, because the lot is patrolled after dark.

senses.definition: Synonym of stallsman (“an accomplice”).
senses.example: Don't trust him, Jack; he's a stall for the crew and always has been.

senses.definition: An action that is intended to cause, or actually causes, delay.
senses.example: His encounters with security, reception, the secretary, and the assistant were all stalls until the general manager's attorney arrived.

senses.definition: Loss of lift due to an airfoil's critical angle of attack being exceeded, normally occurring due to low airspeed.
senses.example: The pilot recovered from the stall by lowering the nose and adding power.

senses.definition: To put (an animal, etc.) in a stall.
senses.example: to stall an ox

senses.definition: To fatten.
senses.example: to stall cattle

senses.definition: To place in an office with the customary formalities; to install.
senses.example: The board will stall the new dean in a ceremony next spring.

senses.definition: To forestall; to anticipate.
senses.example: Their quick apology may stall public anger before it spreads across the city.

senses.definition: To keep close; to keep secret.
To employ delaying tactics against.
senses.example: He stalled the creditors as long as he could.

senses.definition: To employ delaying tactics; to stall for time.
senses.example: Soon it became clear that she was stalling to give him time to get away.

senses.definition: To come to a standstill.
To cause to stop making progress; to hinder; to slow down; to delay or forestall.
To exceed the critical angle of attack, resulting in loss of lift.
To cause to exceed the critical angle of attack, resulting in loss of lift.
senses.example: The pilot stalled the plane by pulling the nose up too high at a slow airspeed.

senses.definition: To plunge into mire or snow so as not to be able to get on; to set; to fix.
senses.example: to stall a cart

senses.definition: To stop suddenly.
To cause the engine of a manual-transmission car or truck to stop by going too slowly for the selected gear.

core.definition: To delay or stop something from moving forward, often on purpose to gain time.

pronunciation.tip: The 'l' is pronounced clearly at the end. Many Americans say it with the same vowel as 'caught', so do not add an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative, depending on context. Stalling is often seen as evasive, but it can also be a strategy for time.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'stall for time' when they want to delay a decision, and 'the car stalled' when an engine stops suddenly. A friend asking why you are late may hear 'Sorry, I was stalling because I didn't want to go.' The noun 'stall' also means a booth at a market or a restroom compartment.

distinctions.note: Delay is neutral and general, while stall often suggests deliberate avoidance or a loss of momentum.
Stop means to end completely, while stall means to halt temporarily or lose motion.

examples.everyday: My kid keeps stalling at bedtime by asking for one more glass of water.
examples.professional: The client is stalling on signing the contract while they review the new terms.
examples.analytical: Opponents of the reform may stall its progress rather than defeat it openly.

nuance.analogy: Like a car engine that suddenly stops because it lost power, a stalled project loses momentum and stops moving.
nuance.etymology: From Old English 'steall,' meaning a place or standing position.
common_mistakes: Using 'stall' only for markets, when Americans use it for stopping or delaying.
Confusing 'stall' with 'stale', which is a different word meaning no longer fresh.

stall.etymology: From Middle English *stall*, *stalle*, from Old English *steall* (“standing place, position”), from Proto-Germanic **stallaz*, from Proto-Indo-European **stel-* (“to place, put, post, stand”).

senses.definition: A complete immobility; a halt.
senses.example: The wreck brought traffic to a standstill for hours.

core.definition: A complete stop, when nothing is moving or making progress, such as traffic that will not move or talks that have stopped.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, STAND. The second syllable 'still' has a short i, like 'bit', so say 'stil' rather than 'steel'. It is one word in American writing.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral; it describes a halt that is usually a problem, like a jam or a failed negotiation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'at a standstill' or 'come to a standstill' for traffic, negotiations, projects, and businesses. 'Bring to a standstill' is common in news reports about strikes or storms. In casual talk, 'it's totally at a standstill' is natural. There is no need for a hyphen, and 'in standstill' is incorrect.

distinctions.note: Halt is more formal and often implies a sudden or deliberate stop, while standstill emphasizes complete immobility.
Deadlock describes a situation where two sides cannot agree, while standstill describes a general stop in activity.
Stop is the general everyday word, while standstill emphasizes that nothing at all is moving.

examples.everyday: The highway was at a complete standstill because of an accident, so we turned around and took the back roads.
examples.professional: Our release has been at a standstill since Monday, until the API team fixes the authentication bug.
examples.analytical: Without a shared definition of justice, the debate reached a standstill that neither side could resolve by argument alone.

nuance.analogy: Like a car with its engine running but its wheels locked: all the power is there, but nothing moves.
nuance.etymology: From 'stand' and 'still', literally meaning to stand still.
common_mistakes: Saying 'in standstill' instead of the American phrase 'at a standstill'.
Writing 'stand still' as one word when it is the verb phrase; the noun 'standstill' is one word.

senses.definition: To remain in one fixed place.
senses.example: I'm not moving there; I'd rather stay put.

core.definition: To remain exactly where you are and not move or change position.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on PUT, and the vowel is the short 'oo' of 'book', not the 'uh' of 'but'. Keep the t sharp at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to firm; it sounds reassuring when asking someone to wait and serious in emergencies.
nuance.usage_note: Americans tell children, pets, and sometimes adults to stay put, as in 'Stay put while I grab the car.' It is casual and sounds comforting when you need someone to wait. In an emergency, officials may say stay put to people who should not move, so it can be a serious safety instruction.

distinctions.note: Stay where you are is more neutral and literal, while stay put is more idiomatic and often used to make a request.
Stay alone means to remain in general, while stay put stresses not moving at all.
Hold still focuses on keeping the body motionless, while stay put focuses on remaining in one location.

collocations: stay put until I call you

examples.everyday: Stay put in the car while I grab the groceries, it'll only be a minute.
examples.professional: Let's stay put with the current vendor until the contract review is finished.
examples.analytical: Some economists argue that workers stay put for too long in declining regions, which leaves them without access to new opportunities.

nuance.analogy: Like a stone resting in one spot while the river flows around it.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'put' like 'putt' or 'but', when the vowel is the short 'oo' of 'book'.
Using 'stay put' in very formal writing, where 'remain in place' is more appropriate.

senses.definition: The property of being stealthy.
senses.example: The stealthiness of the fighter jet allows it to evade radar detection.

core.definition: The quality of moving or acting quietly and secretly, so as not to be noticed or detected.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, STEL, and the th is voiceless. The ending -iness is unstressed and reduced to a short nuss, so do not add an extra syllable or say the -y as a long ī.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can be a positive design feature in military or technology contexts, or a negative trait in covert harm.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this noun mostly in technical or journalistic writing about aircraft, software, or malware, where the quality of being undetectable matters. In everyday speech Americans say 'how quiet it is' or simply use 'stealth' as the noun. The longer form sounds deliberate and analytical.

distinctions.note: Stealth is the common noun for the quality itself and is more natural in most American writing, while stealthiness is a longer, more formal form.
Secrecy refers to keeping information hidden, while stealthiness refers to the quiet, undetected way something moves or acts.
Discretion is careful judgment about what to reveal and is usually positive, while stealthiness describes avoiding detection.

examples.everyday: My neighbor's new car has such stealthiness that you never hear it pull into the driveway.
examples.professional: The security team praised the stealthiness of the new malware, which evaded detection for weeks.
examples.analytical: The critic argued that the novel's stealthiness, its gradual revelation of the crime, is its main artistic achievement.

nuance.analogy: Like the sound of falling snow, stealthiness is the absence of noise, and you notice it only through its effects.
nuance.etymology: From stealthy plus the noun suffix -ness; stealth comes from Middle English stelthe, related to steal.
common_mistakes: Using 'a stealthiness' as a countable noun; it is uncountable, as in 'the stealthiness of the design'.
Saying 'stealthiness' in casual talk where 'stealth' or 'quiet' sounds more natural.

senses.definition: To maintain one’s position or viewpoint when faced with opposition.
(dated) Of a gunner, to persist in faithfully attending to cannons while under fire.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: To maintain your position, opinion, or decision when others criticize or pressure you to change it.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'guns'. 'To' reduces to 'tuh' and 'your' is often softened to 'yer', so the phrase flows as 'stik-tuh-yer-GUNZ'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it praises firmness and integrity, though it can sound stubborn if the position is clearly wrong.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this idiom in work, politics, sports, and family disputes to praise someone who keeps a position under pressure. A typical reply is 'Good for you' or 'That takes guts'. The phrase is informal, so it fits casual and professional talk, but it is less suitable for formal writing.

distinctions.note: Hold your ground stresses resisting physical or social pressure; stick to your guns focuses on maintaining an opinion or decision.
Dig in your heels suggests stubborn refusal to move, often with a negative tone; stick to your guns is usually admiring.

collocations: refuse to stick to your guns
know when to stick to your guns

examples.everyday: My sister wanted to move the wedding date, but she stuck to her guns and kept the original Saturday.
examples.professional: Even after the vendor pushed back, our team stuck to its guns on the security requirements.
examples.analytical: A philosopher who sticks to her guns under objection must still show that the original premise survives the counterexample.

nuance.analogy: Like a soldier holding a position under fire, the person keeps their ground and does not retreat when the pressure rises.
nuance.etymology: Probably from the military image of gunners holding their cannons in position under fire; the exact origin is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Saying 'stick to your gun' in the singular; the idiom is almost always plural.
Pronouncing 'to' as a full 'too' and stressing it.

conversation.text: If you believe the data is right, stick to your guns.
She stuck to her guns and refused to lower the price.
The kids begged for candy, but I stuck to my guns.

senses.definition: In a manner that endures pain and hardship without outwardly showing suffering or expressing complaint.
In an unfeeling manner that inwardly is unaffected by pain or distress.
senses.example: She stoically endured the surgery's recovery without once complaining about the pain.

senses.definition: In a manner consistent with the philosophy of stoicism.
senses.example: Epictetus lived and taught stoically, accepting exile and poverty as matters indifferent to virtue.

core.definition: In a calm, uncomplaining way while enduring pain, loss, or hardship without showing strong emotion.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The final -ally is pronounced as 'uh-lee', with a reduced vowel, rather than as a full 'al-ee'.

nuance.connotation: Positive, since it praises calm endurance. It can suggest emotional restraint that hides real suffering.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use stoically mostly in writing, news, and descriptions of people enduring illness, injury, or disappointment. In conversation, people often say 'She took it really well' or 'He didn't complain.' Stoically sounds more formal, so it fits a story or report better than casual chat.

distinctions.note: Stoically suggests hidden pain or effort to endure, while calmly simply means without agitation.
Bravely is about facing danger or fear, while stoically is about enduring suffering without complaint.

examples.everyday: My grandfather broke his hip and waited for the ambulance stoically, even joking with the nurses.
examples.professional: She stoically accepted the budget cuts and started rebuilding the roadmap around the smaller team.
examples.analytical: The poem's speaker endures exile stoically, refusing to ask for pity or to explain his suffering.

nuance.analogy: Like a rock standing in a river, unmoved by the current that rushes past it.
nuance.etymology: From stoical plus -ly, from Greek stoikos and the Stoa Poikile, where Zeno taught.
common_mistakes: Using stoically where stoic is needed as an adjective, as in 'He is stoically.'
Stressing the final syllable or saying the ending as 'ick-ally' with full vowels.
Confusing the emotional meaning with simply being quiet or silent.

senses.definition: The state or quality of being stony.
senses.example: the stoniness of this soil

senses.definition: The state or quality of being full of stones.
senses.example: the stoniness of this soil

senses.definition: The state or quality of being like stone: immovable, unpersuadable, emotionally cold, or stoic.

core.definition: The quality of being hard and cold, or of being emotionally unmoved, unfriendly, or unyielding.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and keep the endings short: 'nih' and 'nus'. The -ness suffix is a weak, quick sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative in most uses, suggesting coldness, rigidity, or lack of feeling.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'stoniness' mainly in literary criticism, psychology, or formal descriptions of a person's expression or demeanor. In everyday talk, Americans would more often say 'coldness' or 'his cold attitude'. In geology or soil science, the word can also describe ground full of rocks, but that is a technical use.

distinctions.note: 'Coldness' is the common everyday word for an unfriendly or unemotional attitude; 'stoniness' is more literary and emphasizes hardness.
'Sternness' suggests strictness with a serious purpose; 'stoniness' suggests a blank, unmoved, or unfeeling quality.

examples.everyday: I could hear a certain stoniness in his voice when he said he was not interested.
examples.professional: The stoniness of the board's response made it hard for the team to ask follow-up questions.
examples.analytical: The poem links the stoniness of the speaker's heart to a failure of compassion, rather than to any natural hardness.

nuance.analogy: Stoniness is like a riverbed that the water can no longer move: hard, fixed, and unyielding.
nuance.etymology: From 'stony' with the suffix -ness, meaning the state or quality of.
common_mistakes: Using 'stoniness' in everyday talk where 'coldness' sounds more natural.
Confusing it with 'stoniness' meaning ground full of rocks, which is a technical sense.

senses.definition: The plot of a story; one of several within a story, usually interwoven.
senses.example: That film had a wonderful storyline, but the poor acting let it down.

senses.definition: A narrative description of a given modeling scenario, highlighting its main characteristics and underlying technical and socioeconomic drivers.
senses.example: The analysts built a storyline where rising sea levels reduce coastal property values by 2050.

core.definition: The sequence of events that forms the plot of a story, film or show; in data work, a narrative description of a modeling scenario.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on story, and line has a lighter secondary stress with a long i, like the i in fine. Keep the r clear in story and do not split the compound into separate words.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes content without judgment, though a predictable storyline can be criticized.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English, storyline means the plot of a movie, book or TV series, as in the storyline was predictable. In data science and modeling, it is a narrative that explains a scenario's assumptions and drivers to nontechnical stakeholders. In casual conversation, plot is a common synonym.

distinctions.note: Plot emphasizes the causal sequence of events; storyline emphasizes the thread of events, including subplots and interwoven threads.
In modeling, a scenario is the set of assumptions and inputs; a storyline is the narrative that explains them to readers.

examples.everyday: I couldn't follow the storyline of that new show, so I just watched the fight scenes.
examples.professional: Before we run the simulation, please write a short storyline that explains what the demand shock looks like.
examples.analytical: The model's storyline assumes that consumer confidence falls before spending, an empirical claim the data should test.

nuance.analogy: A storyline is like a route description on a hiking map: the scenes are the stops, and the storyline explains why each stop matters.
nuance.etymology: From story plus line, a compound noun.
common_mistakes: Writing it as two words, story line, in formal writing; the standard form is one word.
Using storyline for a single event; it refers to the overall sequence of events.

senses.definition: The act or practice of stowing.
senses.example: the stowage of cargo

senses.definition: A place where things are stowed.
senses.example: Accommodations were so poor I think we were in stowage, with the rest of the cargo.

senses.definition: Things that are stowed.
senses.example: Our stowage disappeared down the chute, into the employee only cargo area, never to be seen again by man.

senses.definition: Amount of room for storing things.
senses.example: The reduction in the ship's size naturally reduced her stowage.

senses.definition: A charge for stowing and storage.
senses.example: We'll have to pay the stowage if we want our crate back.

core.definition: The arrangement or packing of cargo or equipment in a ship, aircraft, or vehicle, or the space used for it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, with a weaker secondary stress on the final syllable, which rhymes with "age." Do not stress the second syllable as strongly as the first.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it describes practical arrangement of goods or equipment.
nuance.usage_note: "Stowage" is mainly used in nautical, aviation, and shipping contexts. In everyday American English, people say "storage" for keeping things in a place. You might hear "stowage" in a maritime training course or a ship's manual, but rarely in casual speech.

distinctions.note: "Storage" is the general word for keeping things anywhere; "stowage" specifically means arranging cargo or gear in a vessel or vehicle.
"Cargo" means the goods being carried; "stowage" refers to how they are packed and placed.

examples.everyday: There isn't much stowage in this little car, so we'll need to leave the cooler at home.
examples.professional: The stowage plan keeps the heaviest containers low in the hold to protect the ship's balance.
examples.analytical: Stowage decisions show how a crew balances safety, efficiency, and limited space under pressure.

nuance.analogy: Like a carefully packed moving truck, where every box is placed to keep the load steady.
nuance.etymology: From stow (verb) with the suffix -age.
common_mistakes: Using "stowage" for ordinary storage in a house; the usual American word is "storage."
Misspelling it as "storage" when you mean the nautical sense of arranging cargo.

senses.definition: To become straight, or straighter.
To steer straight.
To sit up straight, to stop hunching.
To deal with; to put in order.
To tidy; to tidy up.
To clarify.
To start living a reformed life; to adopt a more honest and respectable course of behavior.

core.definition: To tidy a room or space by putting things in order; also to start behaving better after misbehaving.

pronunciation.tip: UP takes the main stress, and STRAIGHTEN is lighter. The n in straighten links into the vowel of up, so it sounds like 'strayt-nup.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral for tidying; it can sound stern when used as a command to a child or someone who is behaving badly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'straighten up' most often for tidying a room before guests arrive, as in 'Straighten up the living room.' It is also a common command to someone misbehaving, as in 'Straighten up or you'll be grounded.' For cleaning dirt or dishes, Americans say 'clean up.'

distinctions.note: 'Clean up' focuses on removing dirt or mess; 'straighten up' focuses on putting things in order.
'Straighten out' means to fix a problem or confusion; 'straighten up' means to tidy or to behave better.
'Shape up' means to improve behavior or performance and is more informal than 'straighten up' in that sense.

examples.everyday: Can you straighten up your room before Grandma comes over?
examples.professional: Let's straighten up the shared folders before the audit so nobody loses track of the final versions.
examples.analytical: The essay tries to straighten up a muddled argument about grace by separating its causes from its effects.

nuance.analogy: Like smoothing a rumpled bedsheet until it lies flat and neat.
nuance.etymology: From straighten plus the particle up, which signals completion or the restoration of order.
common_mistakes: Using 'straighten up' for washing dirt or dishes; for dirt, say 'clean up.'
Confusing 'straighten up' with 'straighten out,' which means to resolve a problem.

senses.definition: A tram or light rail vehicle, usually a single car but sometimes multiple cars attached together, operating on city streets; a trolley car.
senses.example: We rode the streetcar downtown because parking near the stadium was impossible.

core.definition: A passenger vehicle that runs on rails along city streets, usually electric and sharing traffic lanes; also called a trolley car.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, street, and give car a lighter secondary stress. The ar is an American r-colored vowel, like the vowel in the word cot in the cot-caught merger.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, descriptive word, though it evokes older cities and nostalgia.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use streetcar for rail vehicles that run on city streets, especially in cities such as New Orleans, San Francisco, and Boston. Trolley is the more casual word in many places, and the ordinary word for a bus is bus, not streetcar. Tram is rarely used in American English.

distinctions.note: Trolley is more casual and can also mean the overhead pole or a trolleybus, while streetcar is the standard term for the rail vehicle.
Light rail usually runs on its own tracks between districts, while streetcars share city streets with traffic.
A subway runs underground, while a streetcar runs at street level.

examples.everyday: Let's take the streetcar downtown, because parking is a nightmare on weekends.
examples.professional: The city council approved funding to extend the streetcar line to the new medical district.
examples.analytical: The streetcar, once the common carrier of the industrial city, now signals a deliberate choice to shape public life around walkable streets.

nuance.analogy: A streetcar is like a bus that runs on steel tracks, so it always follows the same path.
nuance.etymology: From street plus car, for a vehicle that runs on city streets.
common_mistakes: Calling a bus a streetcar; buses run on rubber tires, not rails.
Confusing streetcars with subways or commuter trains; streetcars run in city traffic at street level.

senses.definition: In a strict manner.
senses.example: He adhered strictly to the diet his doctor prescribed.

senses.definition: In a limited manner; only.
In a narrow or limited sense.
senses.example: That term refers strictly to smaller birds.

senses.definition: In a manner that applies to every member of a set or every interval of a function.

core.definition: Exactly and without exception, following a rule or limit precisely; also used to mean only, for a specific group.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the cluster str-ct-l is said without inserting a vowel, so the t is often nearly silent before the l. Avoid saying STRIK-uh-lee with an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it signals precision or a firm limit, and it can sound stern in phrases like strictly prohibited.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use strictly in two main ways: to mean exactly or precisely, as in strictly speaking or strictly confidential, and to mean only, as in strictly for members. Strictly speaking is a common way to add a qualification or correct yourself, and a natural reply is Fair enough or Good point. Do not use strictly before a noun to mean strict; say strict rules instead.

distinctions.note: Strict is an adjective describing rules or people; strictly is an adverb describing how something is done or limited.
Exactly stresses a precise match; strictly stresses adherence to a rule, definition or limit.
Only is the general word for limitation; strictly adds a sense of formal restriction, as in members-only rules.

examples.everyday: Sorry, the rooftop bar is strictly for guests with reservations.
examples.professional: Access to the production database is strictly limited to the on-call engineers.
examples.analytical: Strictly speaking, the regression shows correlation rather than causation, so the causal claim does not follow.

nuance.analogy: Like a referee who calls only the rules as written, with no leeway.
nuance.etymology: From strict plus -ly; strict comes from Latin strictus, drawn tight.
common_mistakes: Adding an extra vowel in the consonant cluster and saying STRIK-uh-lee.
Using strictly before a noun to mean strict, as in strictly rules instead of strict rules.

senses.definition: Unable to move.
senses.example: Can you shift this gate? I think it’s stuck.

senses.definition: Unable to progress with a task.
senses.example: I’m totally stuck on this question in the test.

senses.definition: No longer functioning, frozen up, frozen.
senses.example: There are several ways to close a stuck program.

core.definition: Unable to move, or unable to make progress; caught in a place, situation, or problem.

pronunciation.tip: This is one syllable with a short u as in cup, followed by a hard k. Do not stretch it into a long vowel like stook or stock; the sound ends sharply.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative; it signals frustration or being trapped, but in everyday speech it is often lighthearted.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use stuck constantly: stuck in traffic, stuck at work, stuck on a problem, stuck with a bill. It is natural in casual conversation and in workplace talk. In formal writing, use stalled, blocked, or unable to proceed.

distinctions.note: Jammed usually describes a machine or door that is blocked, while stuck can describe a person or any situation that cannot move forward.
Trapped means held in a place with no way out, often by force or danger; stuck is milder and more everyday.

examples.everyday: Sorry I'm late, I got stuck in traffic on the highway.
examples.professional: We are stuck on the data pipeline because the API keeps timing out.
examples.analytical: The argument is stuck because both sides define fairness in incompatible ways.

nuance.analogy: Like a key turned in a lock that will not budge, stuck means something has stopped moving when it should keep going.
nuance.etymology: Past participle of stick, from Old English stician, to pierce or cling fast.
common_mistakes: Confusing stuck with stock, which means a supply of goods or a share in a company.
Using the wrong preposition; say stuck in traffic, stuck at home, and stuck on a problem.

senses.definition: Poorly ventilated; partially plugged.
senses.example: I can’t smell very well today – I have a stuffy nose.

senses.definition: Uncomfortably warm without sufficient air circulation.
senses.example: The conference room was stuffy, so we opened the window for some air.

senses.definition: Stout; mettlesome; resolute.
senses.example: The stuffy little terrier refused to back down, even against the much larger dog.

senses.definition: Angry and obstinate; sulky.
senses.example: Dad was stuffy all evening after losing the argument and wouldn't say a word.

senses.definition: Boring, old-fashioned, uninteresting, over-formal, pompous, very conventional.
senses.example: The stuffy professor droned on as the class lost interest.

senses.definition: Stout; sturdy.
senses.example: The stuffy oak table had survived three moves and still stood firm.

senses.definition: Synonym of stuffed toy.
senses.example: My daughter still sleeps with her stuffy, a worn bunny named Pickles.

core.definition: Poorly ventilated, hot, and stale, or (of people) formal, old-fashioned, and dull in manner.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The final y is a short ee, not eye, and the first vowel is the short uh of cup.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes unpleasant air or a person who seems stiff and humorless, though it can be playful in casual speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say it's stuffy in here to ask for a window to be opened. For people, a stuffy professor or stuffy old boss means someone formal and dull. Stuffy can also mean a stuffed toy in speech with children, but this is less common among adults.

distinctions.note: Stale describes air or food that has lost freshness. Stuffy describes air that is hot and poorly circulated.
Formal is neutral and describes correct behavior. Stuffy is negative and suggests that the formality is excessive or dull.

examples.everyday: It's so stuffy in here; can we open a window?
examples.professional: The conference room is stuffy, so I'd suggest we move the meeting to the larger room on the third floor.
examples.analytical: The stuffy manners of the nineteenth-century academy strike modern readers as formal and out of touch.

nuance.analogy: A stuffy room is like a closed car on a summer day: the air is still, warm, and heavy.
nuance.etymology: From stuff (verb), in the sense of to fill up closely.
common_mistakes: Confusing stuffy with stuffed; stuffed describes something filled, while stuffy describes air or manners.
Stressing the second syllable; keep the stress on STUH-fee.

senses.definition: Actually existing.
Inherent.
senses.example: The subsistent virtues of the community, such as hospitality, were visible to every new arrival.

core.definition: Having actual, independent existence; existing in its own right, not dependent on something else.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on 'SIS', and the final '-ent' is only lightly stressed, so use a reduced vowel rather than a full 'ent' like 'rent'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a technical term in philosophy and theology with no positive or negative charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans almost never use subsistent in conversation. It appears in philosophy, theology and older texts, especially when discussing substances, persons or God. For ordinary meanings, use 'real', 'existing' or 'independent'. Use it in a seminar or paper, and expect listeners to ask what you mean.

distinctions.note: Existent means simply existing, while subsistent emphasizes existing on its own, without needing another thing to support it.
Inherent means built into something as a basic quality, while subsistent means having independent being, a term from metaphysics.

examples.professional: Our architecture document describes components as subsistent when they can run without depending on the central service.
examples.analytical: Thomas Aquinas argues that God alone is subsistent being, since every creature receives its existence from another.

nuance.analogy: Like a stone standing on its own, not held up by a wall or a rope.
nuance.etymology: From Latin subsistens, present participle of subsistere, to stand firm; the adjective is used in scholastic philosophy.
common_mistakes: Using subsistent to mean 'living on very little'; that meaning belongs to the verb 'subsist'.
Giving the final syllable a full vowel; it should be a reduced 'ent'.

senses.definition: Able to suffer, endure, or tolerate.
Capable of being endured, tolerated, permitted, or allowed.
senses.example: The heat in the lecture hall was barely sufferable, so we opened every window.

core.definition: Bearable enough to endure; tolerable, not so painful or unpleasant that it cannot be put up with.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, SUF. The middle 'er' is quick and r-colored, and the final '-able' reduces to 'uh-buhl.' Keep the middle and last vowels short rather than giving each a full sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative; it suggests grudging acceptance rather than enjoyment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'sufferable' mostly in writing, especially in reviews and commentary, where it sounds slightly literary. In speech, people usually say 'bearable' or 'not too bad.' 'Sufferable' often appears in negative contexts, such as 'The heat was barely sufferable.' Use it when you want a precise, slightly elevated word.

distinctions.note: Bearable is the everyday word for something you can stand; sufferable is more formal and literary, and often appears with a negative, as in 'barely sufferable.'
Tolerable means acceptable or adequate, often describing quality; sufferable focuses on enduring pain or discomfort.
Insufferable means unbearably unpleasant or arrogant; it is the strong opposite of sufferable.

examples.everyday: The heat is finally sufferable now that the sun is going down.
examples.professional: The office was sufferable during the day, but the ventilation problem made late nights nearly unbearable.
examples.analytical: The regime's policies made daily life sufferable only for those who had already accepted its terms.

nuance.analogy: A sufferable pain is like a loose tooth: uncomfortable and annoying, but you can still chew your food.
nuance.etymology: From 'suffer' plus the suffix '-able,' meaning able to be suffered.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'sufferable' with 'insufferable' and using it for a situation that is truly unbearable.
Stressing the middle syllable, as in suf-FER-uh-ble, instead of the first syllable.

sufferable.etymology: From Middle English *sufferable*, *souffrable* (“bearable, endurable, tolerable; allowable, permissible; able to or willing to bear hardship; forbearing, long-suffering; calm, self-restrained, slow to anger; capable of suffering”), from Anglo-Norman…

senses.definition: Asphyxia—a condition in which an extreme decrease in the concentration of oxygen in the body accompanied by an increase in the concentration of carbon dioxide leads to loss of consciousness or death.
senses.example: A child left unattended may die of suffocation.

senses.definition: A particular act of death or killing by means of asphyxia.
senses.example: The coroner reported three suffocations last week.

core.definition: Death or serious harm caused by a lack of oxygen, often because the airway is blocked or a person breathes in a gas.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on KAY, in the -ation syllable. The first vowel is the 'uh' of 'strut', not a schwa with a different sound. The final -tion is pronounced 'shun'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It names a serious danger, often in safety warnings and news reports.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use suffocation mainly in medical reports, safety labels and news about accidents, such as warnings on plastic bags or cribs. In daily speech, people more often say 'could choke' or 'can't breathe' instead. Use the word for a precise danger, not for a general discomfort.

distinctions.note: Asphyxia is the medical term for oxygen deprivation. Suffocation is the everyday word for the same process, especially when caused by blocked breathing.
Strangulation involves pressure on the neck. Suffocation can occur without any pressure on the neck, such as when the airway is blocked.

examples.everyday: The warning on that plastic bag says it poses a suffocation risk for babies, so keep it out of the crib.
examples.professional: The safety report lists suffocation as the leading cause of injury for that equipment category, so we need redesigned covers.
examples.analytical: The novelist uses suffocation as a metaphor for a life stripped of meaningful choice, where the character cannot breathe in the narrow world she has been given.

nuance.analogy: Suffocation is like a fire going out when the oxygen is cut off: the flame cannot continue without air.
nuance.etymology: From suffocate, from Latin suffocare, 'to choke'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in 'SUF-uh-kay-shun', instead of the -KAY- syllable.
Pronouncing the first vowel as 'oo', as in 'soo-fo-KAY-shun'.

suffocation.etymology: Middle English *suffocation*, *suffocacioun*, from Middle French *suffocation*, from Latin *suffocatio*.

senses.definition: To imply but stop short of explicitly stating (something).
senses.example: Are you suggesting that I killed my wife?

senses.definition: To cause one to suppose (something); to bring to one's mind the idea (of something).
senses.example: The name "hamburger" suggests that hamburgers originated from Hamburg.

senses.definition: To explicitly mention (something) as a possibility for consideration, often to recommend it.
senses.example: This meeting venue was suggested to us by our boss.

core.definition: To propose an idea, option, or action for someone to consider, or to hint at something without stating it directly.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, JEST. The 'gg' is not pronounced as a hard g plus a j; the sound is a single j, so say suh-JEST, not 'sug-GEST'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'suggest' constantly in polite conversation, meetings, and email, often to soften a recommendation. Phrases like 'I'd suggest...' or 'Could I suggest...?' are polite and common. In a meeting, 'What if we...' is more casual, while 'I'd suggest we...' sounds more professional.

distinctions.note: 'Propose' is more formal and often implies a formal plan or offer; 'suggest' is softer and more tentative.
'Imply' means to hint at something without stating it, while 'suggest' can mean either proposing an idea or hinting at one.
'Recommend' means you strongly endorse an option; 'suggest' is weaker and leaves more room for others to disagree.

examples.everyday: Could I suggest we get Thai food instead of pizza tonight?
examples.professional: I'd suggest we review the model's error rates on the new data before we deploy it to production.
examples.analytical: Paul's letters suggest a close connection between faith and obedience, although scholars debate the precise nature of that connection.

nuance.analogy: To suggest is like leaving a note on the table rather than giving an order: the other person can pick it up, consider it, or leave it there.
nuance.etymology: From Latin suggerere, to bring under, supply, or prompt.
common_mistakes: Saying 'sug-GEST' with a hard g, instead of suh-JEST.
Using 'suggest' with a 'to' object as in 'suggest to him that...' when American speakers usually write 'suggest that...' or 'suggest him...' only with a noun object.

suggest.etymology: Coined based on Latin *suggestus*, perfect passive participle of *suggerō* (“bring up, bring under, lay beneath, furnish, supply, excite, advise, suggest”), from *sub* (“from below, under”) + *gerō* (“bear, carry”).

senses.definition: Of, or relating to sulfur, especially in its higher oxidation state.

core.definition: Relating to sulfur in its higher oxidation state, especially in sulfuric acid, H2SO4, a strong acid used in batteries and industry.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the middle syllable, FYOOR, and say the vowel as a 'yoo' sound followed by a clear American r. Learners often say sul-FUR-ik, which sounds wrong to American ears.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a technical term, but sulfuric acid is dangerous, so the word may carry a warning tone in everyday use.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say sul-FYOOR-ik, with a clear r. The word is used almost only in chemistry, industry, and safety warnings, often with the word acid. Do not confuse it with sulfurous, which refers to a lower oxidation state of sulfur.

distinctions.note: Sulfuric refers to the higher oxidation state of sulfur, as in sulfuric acid, while sulfurous refers to the lower state, as in sulfurous acid.

examples.everyday: The battery label warns that it contains sulfuric acid, so don't open it.
examples.professional: The plant produces sulfuric acid for fertilizer, and the safety team tracks every leak.
examples.analytical: Sulfuric acid is a strong diprotic acid, which makes it useful both in industry and as a teaching example in acid-base chemistry.

nuance.analogy: If sulfur is a family, sulfuric is the fully grown, most powerful member, with the highest oxidation state.
nuance.etymology: From sulfur (from Latin sulphur) with the adjective suffix -ic.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like sulfur, as SUL-fer-ik.
Writing sulphuric, the British spelling.
Using sulfuric and sulfurous as synonyms.

senses.definition: Superableness; the ability of an obstacle to be overcome.
Exceptional ability.

core.definition: Exceptional ability; a capacity to do or overcome things far beyond the normal range.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the syllable 'bil,' as in 'ability,' not the first syllable. Keep the middle syllables reduced to 'uh' and end with a clear 'tee.'

nuance.connotation: Positive and admiring, but the word is rare and can sound stilted.
nuance.usage_note: In modern American English 'superability' is uncommon and sounds literary or ornate. Americans would normally say 'exceptional ability,' 'extraordinary talent,' or 'superhuman ability.' The older sense, 'the quality of being overcomable,' is almost never used today.

distinctions.note: 'Ability' is the everyday word for skill or capacity; 'superability' adds the sense of going far beyond the ordinary.
'Superhuman' suggests a power beyond human limits; 'superability' is milder and describes unusually high talent.

examples.everyday: Watching her juggle three projects and still make dinner showed a kind of superability I can only admire.
examples.professional: The team lead's superability to hold the whole architecture in her head made the migration possible.
examples.analytical: Some theologians speak of human superability as a gift, but they insist that it must always be measured against dependence on grace.

nuance.analogy: Like a runner who clears hurdles that would stop most people, the quality shows in what they can get over.
nuance.etymology: From super- (above, beyond) plus ability, from Latin habilis (able to handle).
common_mistakes: Using 'superability' in everyday speech where 'superpower' or 'exceptional talent' would be more natural.
Stressing the first syllable, as in 'SOO-per-ability.'

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to a superhero; reminiscent of a superhero.
senses.example: Her superheroic efforts to finish the marathon with a broken ankle amazed the whole crowd.

core.definition: Like a superhero; showing extraordinary courage, strength or ability, as a superhero would.

pronunciation.tip: Stress ROH, the fourth syllable, with a lighter stress on soo. The -ic ending is 'ik', not 'eek', and the r is clearly pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Positive and admiring; can be playful, sincere or slightly ironic.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use superheroic in casual praise or in conversations about comics and movies, as in a superheroic effort. It can sound flashy or exaggerated, so use it when you truly mean a remarkable effort. In formal writing, heroic is usually better.

distinctions.note: Heroic is the normal word for courage or bravery; superheroic adds a comic-book flavor of extraordinary powers.
Superhuman means beyond ordinary human ability; superheroic suggests the style or spirit of a superhero.
Epic means grand in scale; superheroic focuses on the character-like courage or abilities of a person.

examples.everyday: Pulling my car out of that snowbank during the storm was a superheroic effort, honestly.
examples.professional: Staying on the incident call for eighteen hours was superheroic, but we need a sustainable on-call plan.
examples.analytical: The novel gives its protagonist a superheroic sense of purpose that the prose itself quietly undermines.

nuance.analogy: A superheroic act is like a costume made from ordinary cloth: the feat is real, but the glow comes from the story we tell about it.
nuance.etymology: From superhero plus the suffix -ic, meaning of or like.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable, as in SU-per-hee-ro-ik
Using it as a synonym for superhuman when a literal ability beyond humans is not meant

senses.definition: Of, relating to, or being a surjection.
senses.example: A function is surjective when every element of the codomain is mapped to by at least one input.

core.definition: In mathematics, describing a function where every element of the target set is the output of at least one element of the domain; onto.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, JEK. The first syllable is a reduced, rhotic "ur" sound, and the "j" sound is a soft "dj" in "jet".

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Mathematicians and computer scientists use this word in lectures, papers and proofs. It is usually paired with injective and bijective, and it describes a property of a function, not of a thing. Outside math, you will almost never hear it, so use it only in technical settings.

distinctions.note: A function is injective if different inputs always give different outputs; surjective is about covering the whole target set.
Bijective means both injective and surjective, so each output has exactly one input.

examples.everyday: My nephew is studying for a calculus exam and keeps saying "surjective," and I have no idea what he means.
examples.professional: Before we rely on this mapping in the data pipeline, we need to confirm that it is surjective onto the target schema.
examples.analytical: A function is surjective precisely when its image equals its codomain, so surjectivity is a property of the codomain as much as of the rule itself.

nuance.analogy: A surjective function is like a delivery driver who visits every house on the street: nobody on the list is skipped, though some houses may get more than one visit.
nuance.etymology: Coined in the 1930s by Nicolas Bourbaki from French sur- ("over, onto") and the injective pattern, building on the Latin root for "throw" in function language.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (SUR-jek-tiv) instead of the second.
Confusing surjective with injective, which concerns one-to-one matching rather than covering the target.

senses.definition: Thought, imagination, or conjecture, which may be based upon feeble or scanty evidence; suspicion; guess.
senses.example: surmises of jealousy or of envy

senses.definition: Reflection; thought; posit.
senses.example: Based on the evidence, my surmise is that the outage began after last Tuesday's migration.

senses.definition: To imagine or suspect; to conjecture; to posit with contestable premises.
senses.example: If, as I surmise, you see the ladies this evening, you might mention my intended visit.

core.definition: To guess or infer something from partial evidence, without being certain it is true.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, MIZE, which rhymes with "eyes". Do not stress the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It suggests reasoned guessing, which is less casual than simply guessing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use surmise in written or formal speech, such as reports, mysteries and careful conversation. In casual talk, people usually say guess, figure or think. It is a good word for signaling that your conclusion rests on limited evidence.

distinctions.note: Guess is everyday and can be pure chance; surmise implies reasoning from some evidence.
Infer is standard in analysis and suggests a logical conclusion; surmise is more tentative and less rigorous.

examples.everyday: From the look on her face, I surmise the interview didn't go well.
examples.professional: Based on the server logs, we can surmise that the job timed out before the retry logic ran.
examples.analytical: We can only surmise the author's intent from a few fragmentary letters, and any reading must acknowledge that uncertainty.

nuance.analogy: To surmise is like reading footprints in fresh snow: you can tell where someone probably walked without seeing them.
nuance.etymology: From Old French surmise, meaning "accusation" or "charge," from surmettre, "to accuse," from Latin supermittere.
common_mistakes: Using surmise as a strong claim; it signals tentativeness.
Saying surmise about a fact you already know, which sounds odd.

surmise.etymology: From Old French *surmis*, past participle of *surmetre*, *surmettre* (“to accuse”), from *sur-* (“upon”) + *metre* (“to put”).

senses.definition: Something that provides support or nourishment.
senses.example: Fresh bread and a little cheese were all the sustenance the hikers had left.

core.definition: Food or nourishment that keeps a person or animal alive and healthy, or anything that gives strength.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, SUS. The middle syllables are weak, so the word sounds like 'SUS-tuh-nuns' with a quick, reduced vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It can describe basic food or spiritual nourishment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use sustenance mainly in formal, literary, or religious contexts, or to describe basic food, as in 'a little sustenance for the hike'. In everyday restaurant talk people say 'food' or 'a snack'. It is common in outdoor writing, camping, and sermons.

distinctions.note: Food is everyday and general; sustenance emphasizes nourishment that keeps you going.
Nourishment is slightly more technical or health-focused; sustenance is more formal and may describe spiritual support.

examples.everyday: We packed some trail mix and jerky for sustenance on the hike.
examples.professional: The team relies on the project plan for sustenance, so we must keep updating it as the scope changes.
examples.analytical: Many writers argue that poetry offers spiritual sustenance that prose alone cannot provide.

nuance.analogy: Sustenance is like the oil that keeps an engine running: without it, the whole machine slowly stops.
nuance.etymology: From Old French soustenance, from sustenir, to sustain.
common_mistakes: Using 'sustenance' for a casual snack; in everyday talk 'food' or 'a snack' is more natural.
Stressing the second syllable instead of the first.

sustenance.etymology: From Middle English *sustenaunce*, from Old French *sustenance*, from *sustenir* with the suffix *-ance*, from Vulgar Latin **sustenire*, from Latin *sustinere*.

senses.definition: Furniture with a top surface to accommodate a variety of uses.
senses.example: Set that dish on the table over there, please.

senses.definition: An item of furniture with a flat top surface raised above the ground, usually on one or more legs.
senses.example: Set that dish on the table over there, please.

senses.definition: A flat tray which can be used as a table.
senses.example: Grandpa ate his soup at the lap table in front of the television.

senses.definition: A supply of food or entertainment.
senses.example: The baron kept a fine table and often held large banquets.

senses.definition: A booth or display at an event such as an exposition or fair.
senses.example: Our bakery rented a table at the county fair to sell pies.

senses.definition: A service of Holy Communion.
senses.example: The pastor invited everyone to the Lord's table for the first Sunday service.

senses.definition: The board or table-like furniture on which a game is played, such as snooker, billiards, or draughts.
senses.example: We set up the pool table after dinner and racked the balls.

senses.definition: One half of a backgammon board, which is divided into an inner and outer table.
senses.example: She moved her last checker into the outer table before rolling again.

senses.definition: A group of people at a table, for example, for a meal, meeting or game; a meeting at a table.
senses.example: Time to come to table.

senses.definition: The act of assembling to eat; a gathering to eat, especially at a restaurant.
senses.example: Time to come to table.

senses.definition: The lineup of players at a given table.
senses.example: That's the strongest table I've ever seen at a European Poker Tour event.

senses.definition: A group of players meeting regularly to play a campaign.
senses.example: Our table has played the same fantasy campaign every Thursday for three years.
