senses.definition: A group of diners at a given table or tables.
senses.example: Table 9 wants another round of beers.

senses.definition: A session or sessions of negotiation or diplomacy; an opportunity or place for negotiations.
senses.example: under the table, on the table, turn the tables

senses.definition: A two-dimensional presentation of data; an enumeration of data or contents.
senses.example: table of contents, tide table

senses.definition: A matrix or grid of data arranged in rows and columns.
senses.example: The analyst pivoted the sales data into a table with one row per customer.

senses.definition: A collection of arithmetic calculations arranged in a table, such as multiplications in a multiplication table.
senses.example: The children were practising multiplication tables.

senses.definition: A lookup table, most often a set of vectors.
senses.example: The function checks a lookup table of embeddings before computing new vectors.

senses.definition: Any of various flat surfaces or items with a planar surface.
senses.example: Engineers measured the machined steel table to confirm it was flat within a thousandth of an inch.

senses.definition: A tableland; a flat, elevated region.
senses.example: Cattle grazed on the high table above the canyon, far from any river.

senses.definition: The inner and outer plates that make up the cranium bones; the outer table and the inner table (vitreous table).
senses.example: The radiologist noted a fracture through the outer table of the skull.

senses.definition: A wide, flat obstacle for a horse to jump over.
senses.example: The gelding cleared the wide table easily, landing cleanly on the far side.

senses.definition: The top of a stringed instrument, particularly a member of the violin family: the side of the instrument against which the strings vibrate.
senses.example: The luthier glued the spruce table to the ribs after carving the arching.

senses.definition: The flat topmost facet of a cut diamond.
senses.example: The jeweler polished the table of the diamond so the light would flash through.

senses.definition: A flat gravestone supported on pillars.
senses.example: Moss had crept across the flat table tomb, resting on its four stone pillars.

senses.definition: The quadrangle, a space between the heart line and head line.
senses.example: The palmist studied my table and said the head and heart lines were unusually long.

senses.definition: A visual representation of a classification of teams or individuals based on their success over a predetermined period.
A horizontal stratum of rock.
A flat length of bone.
A stringcourse; a band of horizontal molding or other decoration around a building.
A flat surface that supports the slab on which ink is rolled to manipulate its consistency.
(historical) The game of backgammon, or any of several related games.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To tabulate; to put into a table or grid.
senses.example: to table fines

senses.definition: To put on the table of a commission or legislative assembly; to propose for formal discussion or consideration, to put on the agenda.
To remove from the agenda, to postpone dealing with; to shelve (to indefinitely postpone consideration or discussion of something).
senses.example: The legislature tabled the amendment, so they will not be discussing it until later.

senses.definition: To represent a company or organization (at an exposition, fair, etc.), usually at a booth or display.
To put on a table.
To show one's cards face-up, especially during showdown.
To make board hems in the skirts and bottoms of (sails) in order to strengthen them in the part attached to the bolt-rope.
(rare) To supply (a guest, client etc.) with food at a table; to feed.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: A piece of furniture with a flat top, raised on legs, used for eating, working, writing or placing objects.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable. The final syllable is a syllabic l with no separate vowel, so say 'TAY-bul' with the tongue touching the roof of the mouth at the end, not 'TAY-buh-luh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a basic, everyday word with no positive or negative tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use table in everyday life for dining tables, kitchen tables and desks used as tables. For the verb, note a major difference: in American English, to table a motion or proposal means to postpone it, while British English uses the same phrase to mean to propose it for discussion. In American meetings, 'let's table that' means put it aside for now.

distinctions.note: A desk is designed for writing or working at a computer; a table can be for dining, crafts or anything else.
A counter is a high, narrow work surface in a kitchen or store; a table is usually a freestanding piece of furniture for sitting at.
A bench is a long seat without a back; a table is a flat surface, though picnic tables combine both.

examples.everyday: Can you help me clear the table after dinner?
examples.professional: The conference room table seats twelve, so we will need a few more chairs for the afternoon session.
examples.analytical: Philosophers often use the everyday table to ask how objects first appear to us as useful rather than as bare things with properties.

nuance.analogy: A table is the floor of a room's activity: everything else, from food to papers to conversation, happens on top of it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin tabula, a board or flat surface.
common_mistakes: Saying 'sit on the table' when you mean sit at the table for a meal; 'at the table' is the natural phrase for dining.
Using 'table' as a verb in the British sense to mean propose; in American meetings 'to table' means postpone.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew the word is shulchan and in Greek trapeza, both meaning a table for eating. Psalm 23:5 describes God preparing a table before the psalmist in the presence of enemies, a picture of provision and protection. First Corinthians 10:21 contrasts the 'table of the Lord' with the table of demons, pointing to the Lord's Supper as a sacred meal. Luke 22:21 places the betrayer's hand on the table at the Last Supper, showing how intimate that meal was.

senses.definition: Not derived from formal principles of reasoning; based on induction rather than deduction.
senses.example: Her tacit conclusions about customer behavior came from years of observation, not from any formal model.

senses.definition: Implied, but not made explicit, especially through silence.
senses.example: tacit consent ― consent by silence, or by not raising an objection

core.definition: Understood or implied without being stated outright, often through silence, custom, or shared assumption.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, TAS. The second syllable is a short, reduced 'it'. Do not stretch the first vowel into 'TAY-sit'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes an understanding that is accepted without words.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tacit often in business, law, and academic writing, such as 'tacit approval' or 'tacit agreement'. In casual speech people more often say 'implied' or 'unspoken'. Do not confuse it with 'taciturn', which describes a person who speaks little.

distinctions.note: Implicit means implied by context or logic; tacit means understood without any spoken or written statement, often by mutual consent.
Explicit means stated clearly and directly, which is the opposite of tacit.

examples.everyday: Nobody said we had to tip, but there was a tacit understanding that we would.
examples.professional: Her silence in the meeting was taken as tacit approval for the budget change.
examples.analytical: Polanyi's notion of tacit knowledge names what practitioners know but cannot fully articulate.

nuance.analogy: Like a house rule that everyone follows without anyone posting a sign.
nuance.etymology: From Latin tacitus, 'silent', the past participle of tacere, 'to be silent'.
common_mistakes: Confusing tacit with taciturn, which describes a person who talks very little.
Pronouncing it TAY-sit with a long first vowel.
Using tacit to mean stated or formally agreed, which is the opposite meaning.

tacit.etymology: Borrowed from late Middle French *tacite*, or from Latin *tacitus* (“that is passed over in silence, done without words, assumed as a matter of course, silent”), from *tacere* (“to be silent”).

senses.definition: Teasing; tempting, especially that which is beyond reach.
Teasing temptation.
senses.example: The bakery's tantalizing smell of cinnamon rolls made me forget my diet.

core.definition: Very tempting or exciting, especially when the desirable thing seems just out of reach.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the -izing ending is a long i sound, as in lie, followed by zing. Do not reduce the middle syllable to tan-TAL-.

nuance.connotation: Positive when describing food, opportunities or news; frustrating when the thing is hard to reach.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tantalizing in everyday speech to describe food smells, offers and hints, and in business to describe promising results or opportunities. It is never used of a person as an insult, and it is not the same as tantalized, which describes how someone feels. A natural reply to a tantalizing offer is to ask for more details.

distinctions.note: Tempting focuses on the urge to act, while tantalizing focuses on the teasing frustration of something almost within reach.
Enticing suggests attraction that draws you in, while tantalizing suggests attraction that keeps you partly out.
Tantalized describes the feeling of the person who is teased, while tantalizing describes the thing that does the teasing.

examples.everyday: That pie smells tantalizing, but I'm going to wait until after dinner.
examples.professional: The preliminary results offer a tantalizing possibility, but we need more data before we commit to the redesign.
examples.analytical: The fragment offers a tantalizing glimpse of the author's theology, yet its full argument remains beyond reliable reconstruction.

nuance.analogy: A tantalizing offer is like a window display with the item visible but behind glass.
nuance.etymology: From tantalize, from Tantalus of Greek myth, plus the participle ending -ing.
common_mistakes: Confusing the adjective tantalizing with the feeling adjective tantalized: say I was tantalized but The offer was tantalizing.
Using tantalising, the British spelling.
Applying it to a person as a compliment; it is normally used of things, offers and smells.

senses.definition: Tattered.
senses.example: The tatterdemalion coat hung off his thin shoulders as he walked past the market.

senses.definition: A person with tattered clothing.

core.definition: A person whose clothing is ragged and torn, often someone poor or shabby-looking.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the MAY syllable, and the final part is a reduced 'lee-un' rather than 'lee-ahn'. The middle 'er' is a light, rhotic schwa.

nuance.connotation: Negative or mildly mocking, suggesting shabbiness and disorder; it can also be affectionate when describing a cheerful, scruffy character.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word in conversation. It appears mostly in novels, essays, and humorous writing, where a writer wants a vivid, old-fashioned word for a ragged person. Everyday speakers would just say someone is 'ragged' or 'in rags'.

distinctions.note: Ragged is ordinary and common; tatterdemalion is a rare, literary word with a playful or colorful tone.
Shabby describes worn, old-looking clothes or things; tatterdemalion emphasizes torn, ragged clothing on a person.

examples.professional: The marketing team joked that our first prototype looked like a tatterdemalion, but the core design was sound.
examples.analytical: The novelist portrays the revolutionaries as a tatterdemalion mob, undercutting any romantic image of their cause.

nuance.analogy: A tatterdemalion is like a flag that has been through too many storms: still recognizable, but frayed at every edge.
nuance.etymology: Probably from 'tatter' plus an obscure second element; the exact origin is uncertain.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with stress on the first syllable, as in TAT-er-duh-MAL-yun.
Using it for ordinary dirty clothes instead of torn, ragged ones.

senses.definition: Synonym of assessor (“one who assesses a property for tax evaluation”).
senses.example: The county tax assessor visited our house to reevaluate its value for the property tax bill.

core.definition: A local government official who determines the market value of property so that property taxes can be calculated fairly.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the ses syllable of assessor, while tax has a weaker secondary stress. The final -er is a reduced schwa followed by r, so the word ends softly and clearly with an r sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The term is factual and administrative, though people may feel frustrated when they receive a high valuation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tax assessor for the local official or office that values homes and land for property tax purposes. Many counties and cities call it the county assessor or the assessor's office, and in some states the title is combined with collector. When people want to dispute a property valuation, they usually call or visit this office.

distinctions.note: A tax assessor determines how much property is worth, while a tax collector receives and processes the payments.
An appraiser estimates value for a buyer, seller or lender in private transactions, while a tax assessor values property for taxation.

examples.everyday: I called the county tax assessor's office to ask why our house value jumped so much.
examples.professional: The tax assessor's valuation is due next month, so we need updated square footage in the database.
examples.analytical: A tax assessor must treat a neutral estimate of market value as the basis for every parcel, a standard that is hard to meet uniformly.

nuance.analogy: A tax assessor is like a county official who measures each house before deciding how large its tax bill should be.
nuance.etymology: Assessor comes from Latin assessor, 'one who sits beside' as an assistant judge, from assidere, 'to sit beside'; tax comes from Latin taxare, 'to estimate or charge'.
common_mistakes: Stressing tax too heavily, saying TAX uh-SES-ur with equal emphasis on both words.
Confusing assessor with assessor in education, where it refers to a person who evaluates students or programs.

senses.definition: Viscous streaks left on the inside of the glass when certain wines are swirled around before tasting.
senses.example: Thick tears clung to the inside of the glass after she swirled the Cabernet, suggesting a rich, full body.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of in tears (“laughing; in disbelief”)

core.definition: The salty liquid that comes out of your eyes when you cry, or the state of crying.

pronunciation.tip: Make the vowel long and tense, like 'ee' in 'see', but relaxed toward 'ih' at the end, then pronounce the clear American r. It rhymes with 'ears' and 'years'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most uses, but can carry sadness or emotion depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'in tears' to mean crying, as in 'She was in tears after the call.' Phrases like 'burst into tears' and 'fight back tears' are very common in everyday speech. In wine tasting, 'tears' refers to streaks on a glass, but ordinary speakers rarely use the word that way.

distinctions.note: The verb 'tear' meaning to rip is pronounced 'tair' and is not about crying, so context and pronunciation matter.
'Crying' describes the action of making sounds and weeping, while 'tears' names the liquid itself.

examples.everyday: She tried to hold back her tears, but she started crying at the end of the movie.
examples.professional: After the layoffs were announced, several employees were in tears, so the manager paused the meeting for a few minutes.
examples.analytical: Scripture uses tears as a sign of grief, repentance and hope, which makes them more than a simple physical response.

nuance.analogy: Tears are like rain on a window: they gather quietly, then spill over when there is too much to hold.
nuance.etymology: From Old English teares, plural of teare, from a Germanic root related to the verb 'weep'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'tears' like the verb 'tear' that means to rip, which is 'tair'.
Using 'tear' in the singular for a general feeling; English usually uses the plural, as in 'tears', to describe crying.
nuance.biblical_note: In Hebrew the usual word is dimah (דִּמְעָה), 'tear', and in Greek it is dakryon (δάκρυον), 'tear'. In John 11:35 the shortest verse in the RSV says 'Jesus wept', showing that Jesus shared human grief at the death of Lazarus. In Psalm 56:8 the psalmist says God has kept count of his tears, which expresses God's close attention to human suffering. In Revelation 21:4 the RSV says God will wipe away every tear from their eyes, promising an end to sorrow.

senses.definition: To tilt back and forth on an edge.
senses.example: He teetered on the brink of the precipice.

senses.definition: To totter (move unsteadily).
senses.example: The toddler began to teeter on the edge of the curb before her father caught her.

senses.definition: To be indecisive; to hesitate.
senses.example: We teetered on the fence about buying getaway tickets and missed the opportunity.

senses.definition: To be close to becoming a typically negative situation.
senses.example: Despite appearances, the firm was teetering on the edge of bankruptcy.

senses.definition: A teeter-totter or seesaw.
senses.example: The kids spent the whole afternoon taking turns on the teeter at the playground.

core.definition: To balance unsteadily on an edge or to sway back and forth, as if about to fall; also to hesitate between two choices.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle t between vowels is usually a quick flap in American speech, so it sounds close to 'TEE-der'. Keep the final r clearly pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative when used of hesitation or instability. It often describes a precarious situation in a vivid way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'teeter' in both physical and figurative senses: a stack of boxes teetering on the edge of a shelf, or a company teetering on bankruptcy. The phrase 'teeter on the edge' is very common in news writing. The noun 'teeter' refers to a seesaw, but 'teeter-totter' is the more common American word for it.

distinctions.note: Totter means to walk or stand weakly or unsteadily, often because of age or illness, while teeter means to balance on an edge and swing.
Wobble describes a small, shaky movement, often of an object, while teeter suggests a larger, more dangerous balance on an edge.

examples.everyday: The cookie jar is teetering on the edge of the counter, so move it before it falls.
examples.professional: The project is teetering on the edge of a missed deadline unless we add two engineers this week.
examples.analytical: The author shows the narrator teetering between faith and doubt, never settling on either position.

nuance.analogy: Teeter is like a stack of plates balanced on a narrow edge, swaying before it either steadies or falls.
nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain; closely related to totter, both imitative of unsteady movement.
common_mistakes: Saying 'teeter about' or 'teeter over' when 'teeter on' is the natural preposition for an edge.
Pronouncing the middle t as a crisp, separate t sound instead of the quick American flap.

senses.definition: The act or state of being a tenant.
senses.example: The walls were never painted during my tenantry, becoming dingier and dingier as the years went by.

senses.definition: The body of tenants on an estate.

core.definition: The body of tenants, especially farm tenants, who rent and work the land on a large estate.

pronunciation.tip: Stress TEN. The -antry is often reduced to a quick 'un' sound, so the word sounds like 'TEN-tree' in ordinary speech with a light schwa before the r.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to historical. It describes a social group, often in agricultural or historical contexts, and may carry overtones of dependence or hardship.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in historical, literary, or academic discussions of estates, especially in Britain or Ireland, or of the Southern plantation and tenant farm systems. It is rarely used in everyday conversation. The sense 'the state of being a tenant' also exists but is uncommon; 'tenancy' is the normal word for that.

distinctions.note: Tenancy names the state or period of renting; tenantry names the group of tenants themselves.
Peasantry refers to a broader class of rural workers; tenantry specifically refers to people who rent land from a landlord.

examples.everyday: Grandpa talked about the old families on that estate, the tenantry who farmed the land for the lord.
examples.professional: The historian's study of the tenantry in these villages draws on rent rolls and court records from the 1840s.
examples.analytical: The political grievances of the nineteenth-century tenantry shaped the land reforms that followed and redefined the relationship between estates and their workers.

nuance.analogy: Like a neighborhood of renters on one large property, all living under the same owner and sharing the same obligations.
nuance.etymology: From tenant, from Old French tenant 'holding', from tenir, plus the suffix -ry, meaning a collective group.
common_mistakes: Using tenantry to mean one renter; it refers to the body of tenants as a group.
Confusing it with tenancy; tenancy is the state of renting, while tenantry is the collective group.

senses.definition: The characteristic of being tentative.
senses.example: Her tentativeness during the job interview made the hiring manager doubt her confidence.

core.definition: The quality of being hesitant, provisional or uncertain, not yet settled or fully committed.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, TEN. The middle t may be flapped to a soft d sound in American speech, and the final -ness is a reduced schwa.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can be positive when careful, or negative when it suggests a lack of confidence.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'tentativeness' in reports, reviews and careful writing, and it often describes a plan, offer or reaction that is not yet firm. In casual talk people more often say 'hesitance' or 'hesitation' or just describe the person. A natural reply to 'I sensed some tentativeness' is 'Yeah, they're not fully sure yet.'

distinctions.note: Hesitation is a pause before acting, while tentativeness is a general quality of being unsure and not committed.
Uncertainty is a lack of knowledge, while tentativeness is a lack of firm commitment or confidence in what one says.
Caution is deliberate prudence, while tentativeness can come from fear or doubt rather than planning.

examples.everyday: I heard a tentativeness in his voice when he said he might come to the party.
examples.professional: The tentativeness in the forecast reflects how little we know about the new market.
examples.analytical: The author's tentativeness about causation is a virtue, since the data show only correlation.

nuance.analogy: Like dipping a toe into water before stepping in.
nuance.etymology: From tentative, from Medieval Latin tentativus, from Latin tentare 'to try', plus the noun suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'tentative' with 'tentacle', which has a different meaning.
Using 'tentativeness' for a firm agreement, where the word implies the opposite.

senses.definition: Difficult; tough.
senses.example: A testing time lies ahead for the new administration.

senses.definition: The act of conducting a test; trialing, proving.
senses.example: Rigorous testing of the new software revealed three serious security flaws.

core.definition: The process of checking whether something works, performs correctly or meets a standard by trying it out.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TES. The second vowel is a reduced short 'i', and the ending is 'ting' with a clear ng and no final d sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is positive when it leads to quality and negative when it feels like pressure, as with exam stress.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, testing is a general noun for evaluating things, from medical tests to software quality assurance. In schools it usually means standardized exams, as in 'testing season'. The adjective sense 'difficult, tough' is mainly British or literary; Americans would say 'tough' or 'hard' instead.

distinctions.note: A test is a single evaluation, while testing is the broader process or activity of carrying out evaluations.
A trial is an experiment or a legal proceeding; testing is the systematic checking of something against a standard.

examples.everyday: They're doing blood testing at the clinic, so I'm going in tomorrow morning.
examples.professional: Our load testing showed the API slows down at about two thousand concurrent users, so we need to fix the database first.
examples.analytical: Testing a hypothesis against data is a form of falsification, which makes the rigor of the testing procedure central to the claim.

nuance.analogy: Testing is like tasting a soup before serving it: you check quality before it reaches the guests.
nuance.etymology: From test, ultimately from Latin testum, an earthen pot used for refining metals, plus the noun suffix -ing.
common_mistakes: Using testing as an adjective meaning difficult, which is mainly British or literary; Americans say 'tough' or 'hard'.
Pronouncing it TES-ting with a long e vowel instead of a short e.

senses.definition: Synonym of those that have, get.
senses.example: Our city council ignores small shops, since the rich get richer and everyone knows it.

core.definition: Wealthy people gain more money and advantages over time, while poorer people fall further behind, so existing wealth tends to compound.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the final RICH of richer, while the first two words carry lighter secondary stress. The -er is a relaxed, rhotic schwa, not a full air sound, and get often reduces to git in fast speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It usually criticizes inequality or describes an unfair pattern, often said with resignation or irony.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this proverb when discussing money, taxes, housing, business or politics, often to complain that advantage builds on itself. It sounds cynical if said lightly about someone else's success. A natural reply is 'Yeah, that's how it goes,' or 'It really does feel that way.' Sociologists sometimes call a version of this the Matthew effect.

distinctions.note: The Matthew effect is a technical term from sociology, coined by Robert Merton, for how prominent people receive disproportionate credit; the proverb is the everyday version.
Rags to riches describes a poor person rising to wealth, the opposite story; the rich get richer describes the pattern of existing advantage growing.

collocations: as the saying goes, the rich get richer
the rich get richer and the poor get poorer
it's always the rich get richer

examples.everyday: My neighbor bought a second rental house last year, and now he's making more than ever. Yeah, the rich get richer.
examples.professional: Our pricing rewards the largest accounts, so the rich get richer while smaller clients keep leaving for competitors.
examples.analytical: Merton's Matthew effect describes how already prominent scientists receive disproportionate credit, a sociological form of the proverb that the rich get richer.

nuance.analogy: Like compound interest working in reverse for the poor: a head start grows on its own while a deficit grows too.
nuance.etymology: The proverb is traditionally linked to Matthew 25:29 and Matthew 13:12, but its exact English wording's origin is not firmly documented.
common_mistakes: Saying 'the rich become more rich', which sounds unnatural; use 'richer' with the comparative.
Pronouncing richer with a clear 'air' sound instead of the American rhotic schwa.
nuance.biblical_note: The phrase is not in Scripture as such, but it echoes Jesus' teaching in Matthew 13:12 and the parable of the talents in Matthew 25:14-30, especially 25:29, where those who already have are given more. Readers disagree about whether the parable is about economics or about faithfully using what God has given.

senses.definition: From another point of view; on the other hand; on second thought; again.
senses.example: I think I'll take three pairs of shoes. Then again, I only plan to stay two days.

core.definition: Used to add a contrasting thought or reconsider a point: 'on the other hand' or 'on second thought'.

pronunciation.tip: The first word has secondary stress and the second has primary stress on the final syllable. The word again is reduced to uh-GEN, not AH-gain.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly positive; it shows open-minded reconsideration and softens a statement.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say then again in casual conversation to weigh a point against what was just said. For example, 'It's expensive, but then again, it lasts ten years.' A natural reply is 'True' or 'Good point.' In formal writing, use 'on the other hand' instead.

distinctions.note: Then again is casual and often reconsiders your own view, while on the other hand is more formal and presents a genuinely opposing consideration.
On second thought changes or reverses your decision, while then again keeps the first point and adds a qualification.

examples.everyday: The sandwich was a little pricey, but then again, it was huge.
examples.professional: The model's accuracy improved by five points; then again, the validation set was small.
examples.analytical: The argument seems persuasive; then again, it depends on an unexamined assumption about the author's intent.

nuance.analogy: Then again is like a scale that tips one way and then settles back, showing that the weight of each point must be checked.
nuance.etymology: Combines then and again, both from Old English.
common_mistakes: Writing it as one word, thenagain, which is incorrect in standard English.
Using again alone to mean 'a second time' when you mean to reconsider a point.

senses.definition: Pertaining to theocracy.
senses.example: The theocratic government required all public officials to attend weekly religious services.

senses.definition: Conforming to God-rule, by Christian behavior.
senses.example: The church's theocratic vision shaped every member's daily choices about money, family, and work.

core.definition: Relating to a government or community ruled by religious leaders who claim to govern in God's name, using religious law as the basis of authority.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on KRAT, the third syllable, and the first syllable is a light 'thee-uh'. Americans often hear the 'a' in 'krat' as the short 'a' of 'cat', so say KRAT, not KRAHT.

nuance.connotation: Usually negative in American political discussion, where it suggests religious control of the state, though a religious writer may use it neutrally to describe a historical system.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in political science, history, news about countries such as Iran, and debates about church and state. It is seldom used in casual talk. Describing an American policy as theocratic is a strong accusation, so use it carefully. In everyday speech people might say religious government or government run by clergy instead.

distinctions.note: Religious describes any faith or practice; theocratic describes the structure of government in which religious leaders hold political power.
Theocentric describes a focus on God in thought or life; theocratic describes a political system governed by religious authority.
Secular describes government separate from religious authority; theocratic describes the opposite arrangement.

examples.everyday: My coworker said that country is basically a theocratic state, but I think the situation is more complicated than that.
examples.professional: Our policy brief compares secular democracies with theocratic systems to explain how religious leaders gain political power.
examples.analytical: Calling a regime theocratic requires showing that religious authorities hold formal political power, not merely that religion shapes public law.

nuance.analogy: Like a company whose board is made up only of its founder's inner circle, where the rules and the authority come from the same small group.
nuance.etymology: From theocracy, from Greek theos, god, and kratos, rule.
common_mistakes: Using theocratic as a general word for religious, as in 'a theocratic church', which is a different meaning.
Stressing the wrong syllable (thee-uh-KRAT-ik, not THEE-uh-krat-ik).
Confusing it with theocentric, which describes a focus on God rather than political rule.

senses.definition: An apparatus used to measure temperature.
senses.example: The nurse placed a digital thermometer under my tongue and waited for the beep.

core.definition: An instrument that measures how hot or cold something is, such as the air, a person's body, or food.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, MOM, not on the first. The final -er is a fully r-colored syllable, so don't reduce it to a weak 'uh' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a plain, practical word with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use thermometer for body temperature (a fever thermometer), oven and meat thermometers, and outdoor or indoor temperature gauges. In everyday talk, people more often say 'It's 90 degrees' than check a thermometer. When someone is sick, the natural phrase is 'Let me take your temperature' or 'Do you have a thermometer?'

distinctions.note: A thermometer only measures temperature, while a thermostat measures temperature and controls a heating or cooling system to keep it at a set level.
Temperature is the quantity being measured; a thermometer is the device that measures it.

collocations: take someone's temperature with a thermometer

examples.everyday: Hand me the thermometer, please; I think Jake has a fever.
examples.professional: Please calibrate the thermometer before we log the cold-storage readings for the audit.
examples.analytical: Every thermometer measures temperature indirectly, by tracking a property such as expansion or electrical resistance that changes with heat.

nuance.analogy: A thermometer is a ruler for heat.
nuance.etymology: From Greek thermos (hot) and metron (measure).
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (THER-mometer) instead of the second (ther-MOM-eter).
Saying 'temperature meter', which Americans would not understand as the standard term.

senses.definition: Existing in three dimensions.
Having depth, or the illusion of depth, as well as height and width.
Lifelike.
senses.example: A good novel needs three-dimensional characters.

core.definition: Having length, width and depth; existing in three dimensions, or appearing to have depth.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second part, MEN, and the first syllable of three-dimensional carries only secondary stress. Americans reduce the middle syllables to a schwa, so say dih-MEN-shuh-nul, not dye-MEN-shun-al.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: it is a descriptive term, and it can be positive when used to praise realism or depth.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use three-dimensional in science, design, film, and everyday talk, often to describe objects or visual effects. In casual speech people often say 3D, especially for movies and printing. As a praise word for characters or stories, it means that they feel real and complex.

distinctions.note: 3D is an informal abbreviation common in speech and marketing, while three-dimensional is the fuller and more formal term used in writing and technical contexts.
Two-dimensional describes flat surfaces with only height and width, while three-dimensional adds depth.

examples.everyday: The new movie was so three-dimensional that I actually ducked when the dragon flew at the screen.
examples.professional: We need a three-dimensional model of the warehouse layout so the team can plan the shelving before the purchase order.
examples.analytical: A projection of a three-dimensional object onto a plane loses information about depth, so different objects can produce the same image.

nuance.analogy: Like a sculpture compared with a photograph: the sculpture has depth you can walk around, while the photo shows only one view.
nuance.etymology: Combines three and dimensional, from Latin dimensio, measurement.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable of dimensional, as in DI-men-shun-al; the stress is on MEN.
Hyphenating the phrase after the noun, as in the model is three dimensional; the hyphen is used before a noun, as in a three-dimensional model.

senses.definition: A difficult position.
Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see tight,‎ spot.

core.definition: A difficult or awkward situation, especially one with pressure and few good options.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on SPOT, and tight is lighter. The vowel in spot is the American 'ah' sound, the same as in 'cot.'

nuance.connotation: Negative: it describes trouble, but the term is mild and common in friendly talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say I'm in a tight spot when they face a difficult choice or pressure, often asking a friend for help. Natural replies include What happened? or Can I help? The phrase can also describe a narrow place, but that use is rare.

distinctions.note: Jam is informal for a difficult or awkward situation and can sound more humorous or stressed than tight spot.
A fix is a bind or predicament, and it is also informal, but tight spot is a more general term for difficulty.

collocations: get out of a tight spot
put someone in a tight spot

examples.everyday: I'm in a tight spot, so can you cover my shift tomorrow?
examples.professional: The launch slipped, which put the team in a tight spot with the client.
examples.analytical: The dilemma places the agent in a tight spot where every option seems to violate a duty.

nuance.analogy: A tight spot is like a narrow corridor with no clear exit.
nuance.etymology: Tight from Middle English tight; spot from Middle English spot, a mark or place.
common_mistakes: Dropping the article and saying 'in tight spot' instead of 'in a tight spot.'
Using tight spot only for a physical place; it usually means a difficult situation.

core.definition: In the Bible, a young companion and co-worker of the apostle Paul from Lystra, to whom Paul addressed two letters.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The th is voiceless as in think, and the final syllable is a light ee, not ay.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive in religious contexts; also a common male first name.
nuance.usage_note: Timothy is a common American first name, so people will assume you mean the man in the Bible or a friend named Timothy. In church and Bible study, say his name plainly and add that he was Paul's young companion if needed. Many Americans call him Tim.

distinctions.note: Timothy is the English form used in American Bibles; Timotheus is the Greek form.

examples.everyday: My friend Timothy is named after the young companion of Paul in the Bible.
examples.professional: In the sermon series, we studied Timothy's role as a pastor in the church at Ephesus.
examples.analytical: The Pastoral Epistles present Timothy as the designated successor to Paul, which shapes the church order they describe.

nuance.analogy: Like a trusted apprentice who learns the trade from a master and then takes over the shop.
nuance.etymology: Greek Τιμόθεος (Timotheos), meaning honoring God.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing th as a t or d sound.
Confusing Timothy the companion with Timothy as a common first name without context in a Bible discussion.
nuance.biblical_note: Timothy appears in Acts 16:1-3, where Paul takes him on as a companion; his mother was a Jewish believer and his father a Greek. 2 Timothy 1:5 praises his sincere faith, which first lived in his grandmother Lois and mother Eunice. 1 Timothy 1:2 calls him Paul's true child in the faith. Paul also refers to him as a co-worker in 1 Thessalonians 3:2.

timothy.etymology: Named after Timothy Hanson, who carried the seed from New England to Maryland about 1720.

senses.definition: A spike or point on an implement or tool, especially a prong of a fork or a tooth of a comb.
senses.example: Bend the tine of the garden fork back into shape before you start digging.

senses.definition: A small branch, especially on an antler or horn.
senses.example: The deer's antler had six tines, and the hunter counted each one carefully.

senses.definition: Small, diminutive.
senses.example: Grandpa called the kitten a tine thing, no bigger than my hand.

core.definition: A sharp prong or pointed branch, such as one of the prongs of a fork, a tooth of a rake, or a branch of an antler.

pronunciation.tip: It rhymes with mine and line, with a long i. Do not say it like tin, which has a short vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a plain, descriptive word.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say tine mostly for forks, rakes, and deer antlers, and prong is the more everyday word for a fork. The adjective meaning small is archaic or dialectal, so avoid it. Tines are often discussed in cooking, gardening and hunting contexts.

distinctions.note: Prong is the everyday word for a fork's point, while tine is used in more specific or technical contexts such as rakes and antlers.
Tooth is the general word for a sharp projection on a comb or saw, while tine is used for forks, rakes and antlers.

examples.everyday: Be careful with that fork, because one of the tines is bent.
examples.professional: The fabrication drawing lists the rake tines as six millimeters thick, so check the spacing before ordering.
examples.analytical: The antler's tines branch in a pattern that biologists use to estimate the age of a deer.

nuance.analogy: A tine is like the prong of a plug: a pointed part sticking out from a larger base.
nuance.etymology: From Old English tind, meaning prong or spike.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like tin, with a short vowel, instead of a long i.
Using tine in casual talk for any point, when prong or spike is more natural for most objects.

tine.etymology: From Middle English *tine*, alteration of Middle English *tinde*, *tind*, from Old English *tind*, from **tind*, Proto-Germanic **tindaz*, from Proto-Indo-European **h₃dénts* (“tooth, peg”).

senses.definition: A small added amount of color; a small added amount of some other thing.
senses.example: A faint tinge of blue in the gray paint made the wall look cooler.

senses.definition: The degree of vividness of a color; hue, shade, tint.
senses.example: The sunset cast the clouds in a rosy tinge that faded within minutes.

senses.definition: To add a small amount of color; to tint; to add a small amount of some other thing.
senses.example: Her hair was tinged with silver, though she was only forty.

senses.definition: To affect or alter slightly, particularly due to the actual or metaphorical influence of some element or thing.
senses.example: His optimism was tinged by years of disappointment at work.

senses.definition: To change slightly in shade due to the addition of color; to change slightly in quality due to the addition of some other thing.
senses.example: In autumn, the maple leaves tinge orange before they finally fall.

core.definition: A slight added amount of color or quality, such as a faint trace of a feeling or flavor.

pronunciation.tip: This is one syllable with a short i and a soft j sound at the end. Pronounce the n clearly before the j, and do not stretch the vowel into 'teenj'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. A tinge can be positive or negative depending on what is added, such as a tinge of pride or a tinge of regret.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tinge most often for a faint emotional or sensory quality, as in 'a tinge of sadness in her voice.' It sounds natural in both conversation and writing. In everyday talk, people often say 'a little bit' or 'a hint of' instead.

distinctions.note: Tint is a literal, paler shade of a color; tinge is often figurative and describes a faint added quality.
A hint is a small suggestion or clue; a tinge is a faint quality already mixed into something.
Tingle is a physical prickling sensation on the skin; tinge has nothing to do with physical feeling.

examples.everyday: Her voice had a tinge of sadness when she mentioned her dad.
examples.professional: The early results showed a slight tinge of bias, so we need to check the sample before launch.
examples.analytical: Her argument carries a tinge of nostalgia that colors her whole view of modern life.

nuance.analogy: A tinge is like one drop of food coloring in a glass of water: you notice it, but it does not change the whole thing.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English tingen, from Latin tingere, to dye or moisten.
common_mistakes: Saying the final sound as a hard g instead of the soft j sound
Using tinge for a large amount, when it always implies something small

tinge.etymology: The verb is derived from Latin *tingere*, present active infinitive of *tingō* (“to dip; to moisten; to colour, dye, tinge”).

senses.definition: Resembling or adorned with tinsel.
Gaudy, superficial; offering attraction without depth.

core.definition: Resembling tinsel; cheap, showy and attractive on the surface but lacking real value or depth.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle syllable is a reduced uh sound, and the final syllable is a clear long ee.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It criticizes things that look valuable but are cheap or superficial.
nuance.usage_note: Tinselly is a rare literary adjective, mainly found in reviews, essays or memoirs about glamor and appearances. Americans more often say cheap, flashy or showy in everyday speech. Use tinselly in writing to make a precise critical point.

distinctions.note: Tinsel is the noun for the decoration; tinselly is the adjective for something that looks like tinsel.
Flashy means eye-catching and bright; tinselly adds that the thing is also cheap and shallow.
Gaudy means excessively bright or ornate; tinselly stresses a cheap shine with no real substance.

examples.everyday: The hotel room looked fancy, but the tinselly gold trim was peeling off the mirror.
examples.professional: The marketing deck relied on tinselly buzzwords that promised a lot and delivered nothing measurable.
examples.analytical: Her memoir exposes the tinselly glamor of celebrity life, where applause hides an emptiness at the center.

nuance.analogy: Tinselly is like a plastic bouquet: it looks like real flowers from across the room, but it has no life.
nuance.etymology: From tinsel, plus the suffix -y, meaning having the qualities of.
common_mistakes: Using tinselly as a verb, when the verb is tinsel
Applying it to real gold or silver, which is not tinselly

senses.definition: In need of some rest or sleep.
Fed up, annoyed, irritated, sick of.
senses.example: I'm tired of this

senses.definition: Overused, cliché.
senses.example: a tired song

senses.definition: Old and worn.
senses.example: a tired-looking hotel room

senses.definition: Played out, ineffectual; incompetent.
senses.example: Critics said the senator's tired speeches had grown stale and ineffective.

core.definition: Needing sleep or rest; having little energy after work, activity or lack of sleep.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and pronounce the ending d clearly, as in 'tired'. The vowel of the second syllable is a light r-colored sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes ordinary tiredness; with 'of' it can sound irritated.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use tired to describe normal fatigue, such as 'I'm so tired after the flight.' With 'of', as in 'I'm tired of waiting,' it expresses impatience or annoyance, so use it carefully with bosses or customers. A natural reply is 'Get some rest' or 'Me too.'

distinctions.note: Exhausted is stronger and means completely drained, while tired is a general word for needing rest.
Sleepy specifically means wanting to sleep, while tired can refer to physical or mental fatigue.

examples.everyday: I'm really tired tonight, so I'm going to bed early.
examples.professional: After three late releases, the team is tired, so let's push the hard decisions to next sprint.
examples.analytical: The argument has grown tired, relying on familiar slogans rather than new evidence.

nuance.analogy: Like a phone battery that is down to five percent and needs a charge.
nuance.etymology: Past participle form of the verb tire, meaning to make weary or to become weary.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I am tire' instead of 'I am tired'.
Saying 'tired to wait' instead of 'tired of waiting'.

conversation.text: I'm so tired. I was up all night with the baby.
You look tired. Do you want to sit down?
I'm tired of eating the same thing every day.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of Tommy Atkins, a typical private in the British army; a British soldier.
Any common soldier; a member of the rank and file.
Ellipsis of tommy boy.
Penis.

core.definition: A familiar nickname for a man or boy named Thomas.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final 'y' is pronounced like the long 'ee' of 'see', not 'eye'. The 't' is a clear, aspirated 't', not a flap.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to friendly. As a nickname it is warm and casual, though the British-army sense is historical and can seem old-fashioned.
nuance.usage_note: In the United States Tommy is mainly a nickname or first name, and it is used freely in conversation, such as 'Tommy, dinner is ready.' The old sense of a British soldier, from Tommy Atkins, is mostly known through history and British culture, and Americans would more likely say soldier or GI for a common soldier. Americans may also recognize the Tommy gun, a historic submachine gun.

distinctions.note: Tom is a shorter, more common nickname for Thomas, and Tommy is a more affectionate or childlike version.
Thomas is the formal full name, often used in official contexts, while Tommy is a casual nickname.

examples.everyday: Tommy, can you grab the milk on your way back from the store?
examples.professional: Tommy from accounting already sent the revised budget, so we can finalize the numbers this afternoon.
examples.analytical: The name Tommy Atkins became a generic label for the British soldier, showing how a single name could stand for the ordinary rank and file.

nuance.analogy: Tommy is like a warm, friendly version of Thomas, the way a coat with a soft lining is a friendlier version of the same coat.
nuance.etymology: A diminutive of Thomas; the soldier sense comes from Tommy Atkins, a sample name used on British army forms in the 1800s.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final 'y' as 'eye' instead of 'ee'.
Using Tommy for a British soldier in American conversation, where it sounds oddly historical.

senses.definition: Relating to barbering, shaving, or hairdressing.

core.definition: Relating to barbers, barbering, shaving, or hairdressing.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable and reduce the final -ial to a light 'ee-ul'. Do not stress the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to humorous. It sounds formal or playful, often used when describing barbers or barbershops in a witty way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'tonsorial' in everyday talk. It appears mainly in writing, humor, or formal discussions of barbering. A casual speaker would say 'haircut', 'barber', or 'barbershop' instead.

distinctions.note: Barber is the everyday noun for the person, while tonsorial is an adjective describing the trade or its practices.
Cosmetic refers to beauty products or treatments, while tonsorial is specifically about hair cutting and shaving.

examples.everyday: He jokes that his tonsorial training taught him more about people than any class did.
examples.professional: The salon's tonsorial services include cuts, shaves, and beard trims, so we need two barbers on Saturdays.
examples.analytical: Historians of the barbershop trace how tonsorial practice shaped male social life in nineteenth-century American cities.

nuance.analogy: Tonsorial is a fancy umbrella term, like a formal label on a barber's sign.
nuance.etymology: From Latin tonsor, 'barber', from tondere, 'to shear or clip'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as in 'TAHN-sor-ee-al'.
Using it in casual speech where 'barber' or 'haircut' is more natural.

senses.definition: Having prominent teeth.
With the fellator's teeth scraping the fellatee's penis.
senses.example: Hot take, maybe I'm a bit of a masochist but I enjoy some toothy head from time to time.

core.definition: Having large or prominent teeth, or showing a wide smile with many teeth visible.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The th is voiceless, as in thin, not a t, and the ending is a clear ee sound like happy.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly playful. A toothy grin usually sounds friendly or eager, but calling someone's face toothy can sound unflattering.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use toothy mostly for smiles, grins and animals with big teeth, as in a toothy grin or a toothy smile. It is casual and descriptive, and rarely used of adults in a formal way. Toothy also has a crude sexual slang sense in some dictionaries, so avoid that meaning in polite company.

distinctions.note: Buck-toothed describes prominent front teeth that stick out as a physical feature, while toothy is about showing many teeth, often in a smile.
Toothsome is a literary or old-fashioned word meaning tasty or appealing, so it is not used for teeth in modern English.

examples.everyday: The little boy gave me a big toothy grin when I handed him his ball.
examples.professional: Our new hire has a warm, toothy smile that makes the client calls go more smoothly.
examples.analytical: The portraitist exaggerates the toothy grins of the merchants, turning their courtesy into something faintly predatory.

nuance.analogy: Like a piano keyboard opening into a smile, showing many white keys at once.
nuance.etymology: From tooth plus the suffix -y, meaning having or full of.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the th as a t, saying too-tee with a hard t sound.
Using toothy to mean having bad or crooked teeth, when it describes showing teeth.
Using the crude sexual slang sense in ordinary conversation.

senses.definition: Synonym of high-end (“sophisticated or expensive”).
senses.example: The store carries top-end appliances, but most shoppers buy the cheaper models.

senses.definition: Of or relating to the higher gears on a geared engine, especially in a motor vehicle.
senses.example: At highway speed, the truck pulls hard in top-end gears, so you rarely need to downshift.

core.definition: Very expensive and high in quality; at the highest price or level of a product or service range.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on END, and top has a lighter stress. Pronounce the vowel in top as the short American o, the same as in 'cot.'

nuance.connotation: Positive for quality, though it can also suggest a high price. In a shopping context, it often signals that a product is the best available.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use top-end when describing products, restaurants, hotels, and markets, such as 'a top-end laptop.' In everyday speech, high-end is more common, and top-of-the-line is also very natural for products. Top-end is sometimes used for prices or market segments, so it is useful in business conversations.

distinctions.note: High-end is the more common everyday term for expensive, sophisticated goods, while top-end often refers to the highest tier in a range.
Luxury describes an experience of indulgence or rarity, while top-end describes a position at the top of a price or quality range.

examples.everyday: We ate at a top-end steakhouse for her birthday, and the food was worth the price.
examples.professional: Our top-end product line carries the highest margins, so we're focusing sales effort there this quarter.
examples.analytical: Market segmentation often separates top-end buyers, who value design and service, from price-driven buyers.

nuance.analogy: A top-end car is the one with every option package and the most expensive trim.
nuance.etymology: Combines top (Old English topp) and end (Old English ende).
common_mistakes: Leaving out the hyphen before a noun, as in 'a top end restaurant.'
Using it for people, as in 'a top-end person,' where high-level or senior is more natural.

senses.definition: (archaic) Tragic.
senses.label: archaic

core.definition: An archaic form of tragic, meaning sad, dreadful, or ending in disaster; modern English uses tragic instead.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, TRAJ, and the ending is a quick 'ih-kul'. Avoid stressing the second syllable, as in 'tra-JI-cal'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. It sounds old-fashioned and is used mostly for literary effect.
nuance.usage_note: Americans today say tragic, and tragical sounds archaic or deliberately old-fashioned. You might see it in older texts, in Shakespearean-era or Elizabethan writing, or in a book title. In modern conversation, using it would sound quaint or humorous, so stick with tragic.

distinctions.note: Tragic is the standard modern adjective, while tragical is an older form that sounds dated and literary.
Tragicomic describes a mix of comedy and tragedy, while tragical describes only the tragic side.

examples.everyday: Grandpa's old storybook called the tale a tragical one, which made us laugh because nobody talks like that anymore.
examples.professional: The archive catalog lists the 1890 edition under tragical, but the modern subject heading uses tragic.
examples.analytical: Marlowe's The Tragicall History of Doctor Faustus shows an older spelling and adjective that the modern word tragic has largely replaced.

nuance.analogy: Tragical is like a vintage car: the same idea as tragic, but with an older design that people rarely drive today.
nuance.etymology: From Latin tragicus, with the older adjective ending -al, which is an earlier English form of tragic.
common_mistakes: Using tragical in everyday conversation, where tragic is the normal word.
Confusing tragical with tragicomical, which means a mixture of tragic and comic elements.

senses.definition: The act of trampling someone or something, an instance of trampling.

core.definition: The act of stepping on and crushing someone or something heavily underfoot, or an instance of doing so.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the a is the short vowel in trap. The pl is a single blend before the -ing ending, so say TRAM-pling, not TRAM-pal-ing.

nuance.connotation: Negative, since it suggests heavy, damaging crushing, whether physical or figurative.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use the noun mostly for physical crushing, such as a trampling in a crowd, or figuratively for violating rights, as in trampling on someone's rights. In casual talk, people more often use the verb, as in the crowd trampled the flowers, which sounds more natural than the noun form.

distinctions.note: Stomping is an informal, often noisy action with the foot, while trampling suggests heavy, damaging crushing of many things or people.
Violation is a general term for breaking a rule or right, while trampling implies contemptuous disregard, as in trampling on someone's rights.

examples.everyday: After the concert, the trampling near the stage left the lawn a muddy mess.
examples.professional: The report links the trampling of the nesting area by hikers to the drop in bird counts.
examples.analytical: Her argument is that the trampling of basic rights by the emergency decree did more damage than the crisis itself.

nuance.analogy: Trampling is like a herd of cattle crossing a field: the damage is heavy, and it spreads with every step.
nuance.etymology: From trample (Middle English trampelen, from tramp, to tread heavily) with the -ing noun ending.
common_mistakes: Using the wrong preposition: say trampling on rights or trampling through a garden, not trampling to rights.
Using the noun where a verb is needed: say the crowd trampled the flowers, not the crowd trampling the flowers.
nuance.biblical_note: Scripture uses trample for crushing or treading underfoot, often as a picture of contempt or judgment. Matthew 7:6 warns against throwing pearls before swine, lest they trample them under foot, a point about sacred things being despised. Isaiah 63:3 pictures God treading the winepress of judgment alone, and Revelation 11:2 speaks of the holy city being trampled for a set period. Behind these passages are the Hebrew darak (to tread) and the Greek pateo (to tread or trample).

senses.definition: Synonym of solicitor.

core.definition: A lawyer who handles business deals, contracts, mergers and planning rather than courtroom litigation. In the US this is not a synonym for solicitor.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on AK in transactional and on TUR in attorney, so avoid 'tran-sack-SHUN-al' with stress on the end. The r in attorney is strongly pronounced in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and professional, describing a specialty rather than a judgment of the lawyer.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say attorney or lawyer, and solicitor usually means a government law officer, such as the Solicitor General, or a British lawyer. A company might say 'We need a transactional attorney to review the merger agreement.' Clients often call them deal lawyers in casual talk.

distinctions.note: A litigator argues cases in court, while a transactional attorney drafts and negotiates deals outside court.
In the UK a solicitor does the same kind of work as a US transactional attorney, but in America solicitor means a government lawyer or is rarely used.
A paralegal supports lawyers with research and documents but cannot give legal advice or represent clients.

collocations: a transactional attorney for the startup

examples.everyday: My cousin is a transactional attorney, so she helped us read the lease before we signed it.
examples.professional: Let's loop in a transactional attorney before we send the revised term sheet to the buyer.
examples.analytical: A transactional attorney's skill lies in anticipating disputes and drafting terms that prevent them, rather than resolving them later in court.

nuance.analogy: Like an architect who designs a building so it won't collapse, rather than the engineer who repairs it after a storm.
nuance.etymology: Transaction from Latin transigere, to carry through; attorney from Old French atorner, to appoint.
common_mistakes: Calling a US lawyer a solicitor, which sounds British and may confuse Americans.
Assuming a transactional attorney goes to court; most of their work happens in negotiations and documents.

senses.definition: Something which traverses or moves, such as an index on a scale.
Someone who traverses a region.
A traverse table.
senses.example: The navigator used a traverser to plot the ship's course from the logged distances.

core.definition: A person or thing that crosses or moves across a region, or a movable index on a scale.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, VUR, and reduce the first syllable to a weak 'truh'. The final -er is an American r-colored vowel, so it sounds like 'sur'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise term with little emotional meaning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word in everyday speech and would normally say 'traveler' for a person on a journey. In technical settings, such as surveying or instrumentation, it can refer to a device or part that moves across a scale. Use it only when you need the precise sense of crossing a region.

distinctions.note: Traveler is the common word for a person on a journey, while traverser is a formal or technical term that stresses crossing a region.

examples.everyday: He's a frequent traverser of these mountain trails, so he knows every shortcut.
examples.professional: The surveying team used a traverser to record each angle along the boundary line.
examples.analytical: Each generation became a new traverser of the old border, redrawing its meaning as it crossed.

nuance.analogy: A traverser is like a hiker who walks the whole ridge, not just one trail.
nuance.etymology: From traverse plus the agent suffix -er, meaning one who traverses.
common_mistakes: Using traverser when traveler is the normal word.
Stressing the first syllable, as in TRAV-ers-er.

senses.definition: The property or state of being tremulous.

core.definition: The state of being tremulous, meaning trembling, shaky, or easily frightened, especially in voice or feeling.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TREM. The -ous and -ness endings are unstressed, and the 'oo' in the middle is a short, light vowel. Avoid adding an extra syllable before 'ness'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to tender; it describes emotional vulnerability and can be admiring or sympathetic.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this noun in everyday talk. It appears in literary criticism, fiction, and careful description of a person's feelings. In conversation, say 'nervousness' or 'shakiness' for the same idea.

distinctions.note: Nervousness is the general everyday word for anxiety. Tremulousness focuses on the trembling or fragile quality that shows in voice or movement.
Timidity is a character trait of shyness. Tremulousness can be temporary and visible, like a shaky voice at a moment of stress.

examples.professional: The tremulousness of her first presentation faded once she found her footing with the data.
examples.analytical: Kierkegaard's prose draws much of its power from a tremulousness before the absolute, a fear that also shapes faith.

nuance.analogy: Like a candle flame in a draft, it flickers without going out.
nuance.etymology: From tremulous, from Latin tremulus 'trembling', plus the English suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Confusing tremulousness with tremendousness, which is a different word with different meaning.
Stressing the wrong syllable; keep the main stress on TREM.

senses.definition: A small, showy ornament, especially a piece of jewelry.
senses.example: That little trinket around her neck must have cost a bundle.

senses.definition: A thing of little practical and/or monetary value; a toy, a trifle.
senses.example: It’s only a little trinket, but it reminds her of him.

senses.definition: A small item of food; a small dainty.
senses.example: Grandma offered each child a sweet trinket of candied almond after dinner.

senses.definition: A small item forming part of a set of equipment; an accessory, an accoutrement.
senses.example: The camera kit included a tripod plate and various trinkets for quick setup.

senses.definition: An item used in a religious rite (also, a religious rite, belief, etc.) regarded as superfluous or trivial.
senses.example: The reformer dismissed the relics and rosaries as mere trinkets of a faltering faith.

senses.definition: (rare) Often followed by out: to adorn (someone or something) with trinkets (noun etymology 1, noun sense 1).
senses.example: They trinketed the altar out with ribbons, bells, and tiny silver charms.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: A small, decorative object of little monetary value, such as a cheap piece of jewelry, a souvenir, or a small ornament.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and say the ng and k together. The final -et is a weak vowel, so it sounds like TRINK-uht, not TRINK-et.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative. It suggests something cheap or sentimental rather than valuable.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use trinket for small souvenirs, cheap jewelry, and decorative objects sold in gift shops. Calling a present just a little trinket is a modest, polite way to give something small. For valuable items, say jewelry or heirloom instead.

distinctions.note: A knickknack is a small decorative household object, often displayed on a shelf, and is more everyday than a trinket.
Jewelry is usually more valuable and worn, while a trinket is cheap, decorative, or sentimental.
A trifle is anything unimportant, not necessarily decorative, while a trinket is a physical object.

examples.everyday: I bought a few little trinkets at the gift shop for my nieces.
examples.professional: We cut the trade-show budget and dropped the trinkets, focusing on the product demo.
examples.analytical: Modern consumer culture turns many objects into trinkets whose worth depends on memory rather than material.

nuance.analogy: Like a souvenir from a museum gift shop: small, pretty, and meaningful mainly to the person who keeps it.
nuance.etymology: Of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable (trin-KET) instead of the first (TRINK-uht).
Using trinket for valuable items; for precious objects say jewelry or heirloom.

trinket.etymology: The origin of the noun is; the word is possibly related to.

senses.definition: The characteristic of being true.
Loyalty; faithfulness; constancy.
senses.example: Despite the rumors, nobody doubted his trueness to the church that raised him.

core.definition: The quality of being true, accurate, or exact, such as the precision of a shape or measurement, or the faithfulness of a thing.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and pronounce the final -ness as a soft nus. Keep the oo vowel long and round, and avoid adding an extra vowel between n and s.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes accuracy or faithfulness without strong emotion.
nuance.usage_note: Trueness is rare in everyday American speech. Americans would usually say accuracy, precision, truth, or fidelity. It is still used in engineering and mechanics, especially for the straightness or alignment of a part such as a wheel. Outside technical contexts, it sounds literary and slightly old-fashioned.

distinctions.note: Accuracy is the everyday word for how close a measurement or statement is to the correct value, while trueness is more technical and often refers to shape or alignment.
Truth is a general noun for what is real or a statement that is correct, while trueness describes the quality or degree of being true or aligned.
Fidelity emphasizes faithfulness to an original or to a promise, while trueness can describe physical alignment or accuracy.

collocations: check the trueness of the wheel

examples.everyday: The mechanic checked the trueness of my bike wheel before I rode it, because the rim wobbled a bit.
examples.professional: We need to verify the trueness of the sensor readings before we calibrate the model against the reference data.
examples.analytical: The essay defends the trueness of a belief against both relativism and mere sincerity, arguing that conviction alone does not guarantee correspondence to reality.

nuance.analogy: The trueness of a measurement is like a ruler whose markings line up exactly with the real length of the object.
nuance.etymology: From true plus the suffix -ness.
common_mistakes: Using trueness in everyday conversation where accuracy or truth would sound more natural.
Confusing trueness with truthfulness, which describes a person who tells the truth.
Adding an extra syllable and saying troo-un-ness.

trueness.etymology: From Middle English *trewenesse*, *trewnesse*, from Old English *trēownes*, equivalent to *true* + *ness*.

senses.definition: A test of the suitability or effectiveness of a person or thing, especially an audition for a performer or athlete, or the advance staging of a play at a small theater.
senses.example: She nervously waited for the tryout before the coach picked the starting lineup.

core.definition: A test of whether a person or thing is suitable, such as an audition, a trial for a team, or a short trial period.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable in the noun, 'TRY-owt'. In the phrasal verb 'try out', the stress shifts to 'out', so keep the stress shift in mind.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes an evaluation and is not negative, though a tryout can feel stressful.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'tryout' most often in sports, music, and theater, as in 'open tryouts for the varsity team'. For a job, Americans usually say 'interview' or 'trial period', though 'tryout' can describe a short test assignment. The phrasal verb 'try out for' is the common way to say you are going to a tryout.

distinctions.note: 'Audition' is for performers such as actors and singers, while 'tryout' is broader and common in sports.
'Trial' often means a legal proceeding or a longer test period, while 'tryout' is a brief test of ability.
A 'preview' is a public showing before a play or film opens, while a 'tryout' is an evaluation of a performer or team.

examples.everyday: Tryouts for the varsity soccer team are next Monday, so you'd better start running now.
examples.professional: The new vendor is in a two-week tryout before we sign the contract, so we'll know more by the end of the month.
examples.analytical: A tryout of the new policy in one region reveals more about its real effects than its written justification does.

nuance.analogy: A tryout is like a dress rehearsal for a job: the real performance comes later, but this shows whether you can do it.
nuance.etymology: Formed from the phrasal verb try out (try plus out); the noun form is a later compound.
common_mistakes: Stressing 'out' in the noun ('try-OUT') instead of 'TRY-out'.
Saying 'I'm tryout for the team' instead of 'I'm trying out for the team'.

senses.definition: Any of very many chordate marine animals, of the subphyla Tunicata or Urochordata, including the sea squirts.
senses.example: On the dive, we found a tunicate attached to the rocks, its body covered in a jelly.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to Tunicata or Urochordata.
senses.example: The biologist's paper examined the feeding behavior of tunicate larvae in coastal waters.

senses.definition: Enclosed in a tunic or mantle; covered or coated with layers.
senses.example: The tunicate bulb of the onion has papery layers that protect the tender inner flesh.

senses.definition: Having each joint buried in the preceding funnel-shaped one, as in certain antennae of insects.
senses.example: The insect's antenna is tunicate, with each segment fitting snugly inside the one before.

core.definition: A marine animal, such as a sea squirt, with a tough outer covering like a tunic around its body.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, TOO. The middle vowel is short and reduced, and the final -ate is a light schwa, not a long a as in 'ate'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a scientific term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Biologists, marine scientists and zoology students use tunicate. In everyday American speech, people say 'sea squirt' for many of these animals. The group is also called Urochordata in some scientific texts.

distinctions.note: Sea squirt is the common name for many tunicates and is used in everyday speech, while tunicate is the scientific term.
A chordate is a member of the broader phylum that includes vertebrates, and tunicates are one group within it.
A tunic is a garment, so the word is unrelated to the animal except by the shared idea of a covering.

examples.everyday: We saw a sea squirt on the dock, and the guide said it was a kind of tunicate.
examples.professional: Our lab sequenced the genome of a colonial tunicate to study the origin of vertebrate traits.
examples.analytical: Because tunicate larvae have a notochord in the tail, they are central to debates about the evolutionary path toward vertebrates.

nuance.analogy: A tunicate is like a small sack of seawater with a tough coat, filtering food from the water as it passes through.
nuance.etymology: From Latin tunica, 'tunic', referring to the outer covering.
common_mistakes: Mistaking tunicate for tunic, the piece of clothing, since the words look alike.
Using tunicate in casual talk, where 'sea squirt' is the usual word.

senses.definition: Action of the verb to tune.
senses.example: The tuning of the old piano took nearly two hours, and my grandmother hummed along the whole time.

senses.definition: The calibration of a musical instrument to a standard pitch.
senses.example: Before the concert, the cellist checked her tuning against the orchestra's A.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of tuning system.
The adjustment of a system or circuit to secure optimum performance.
senses.example: Engineers spent weeks on the tuning of the amplifier circuit to reduce distortion.

core.definition: The process of adjusting an instrument, such as a guitar or piano, so its notes are at the correct pitch.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, TOON. The ending is a short 'ing' with a clear ng sound, not a long i.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a routine, practical process.
nuance.usage_note: Musicians use tuning for adjusting instruments before playing, and car owners may talk about engine tuning. In everyday speech, Americans often say 'tune-up' for routine engine service. Tuning is also used for setting a radio to a station.

distinctions.note: A tune-up is routine maintenance of an engine or device, while tuning is adjusting pitch or frequency.
Calibration is a precise adjustment against a standard, typical of science and measurement, while tuning is more practical and musical.
A tuning system is a set of pitch relationships, such as equal temperament, while tuning is the act of adjusting.

examples.everyday: Give me a minute for tuning, and then we can start playing.
examples.professional: The sound engineer booked two hours for tuning the drum kit before the recording session.
examples.analytical: Historical tuning systems shaped which intervals sounded consonant, so tuning has never been purely mechanical.

nuance.analogy: Tuning a string is like adjusting a bicycle chain: a small turn changes how the whole thing runs.
nuance.etymology: From tune plus the suffix -ing, forming a noun from the verb.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I am tuning to the station' in the sense of setting a radio; Americans say 'I'm tuned to' or 'I tuned in to' a station.

senses.definition: To become.
senses.example: all things turn into dust

senses.definition: To cause (something or someone) to become.
senses.example: He turned water into wine.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see turn,‎ into.
senses.example: I was just turning into my driveway when I got your call.

core.definition: To become something different, or to make someone or something change into something else.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on in, and the final unstressed to is weak, often 'tuh' in fast speech. Do not stress the second word as in-TOO; in fast talk it sounds like 'turn-IN-tuh'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it can be positive ('turned into a great player') or negative ('the party turned into a mess').
nuance.usage_note: Americans use turn into for gradual change and sudden transformation: 'the weather turned into a storm' or 'my son turned into a teenager overnight.' It is informal and everyday. Remember that turn to means go to someone for help, while turn into means become.

distinctions.note: Become is general and neutral; turn into is informal and often implies a visible or surprising change.
